en: The Essential Source for the Profound Meaning of Nirvāṇa, Scroll One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyuan of Qiantang during the Song Dynasty.
This *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) is the original text of Zhang’an; as its phrasing and purport are already perfect, Jingxi did not [further elaborate upon it].
It was further revised and edited.
Some say that because the subsequent text contains the statement, "One chapter is missing herein," we know it has also undergone a second revision.
Now I say it is not so; the words in the omitted passage were likely annotations added by later people, which the scribe mistakenly transcribed.
These are merely vulgar and commonplace remarks; how could they possibly be examples from Jingxi’s own final revisions?
If it is to be corrected again, one should write:
"The four clarities are neither-arising-nor-non-arising," with the word "missing" (闕) annotated below.
This is like the three major chapters of Master Liang’s *Zhi guan* that were deleted, all of which were annotated as "missing."
Now, examining this through seven points of reasoning, we know that it was not revised a second time.
First, had the commentary been revised a second time, the two characters "Daban" (Mahāparinirvāṇa) would have been deleted from the general title.
Now, since these [details] are all present here, we know it was not re-edited.
Second, because there is no mention of the name of a person who re-edited it beneath the title.

Third, some might argue that it is incomplete; however, even if it were incomplete, if the name of the editor had been omitted, it would be inconsistent for the name of the commentator (shushu) to be so clearly inscribed.
For example, in the sub-commentary below, it should have simply stated "Compiled by Master Ding.
Since his name and style-name are now clearly written, we know it was not re-edited.
Fourth, there are no words of personal opinion at all within the text; thus, we know it was not re-edited.
Fifth, according to the *Vimalakīrti* section, Jingxi also merely abridged the commentary text and did not re-edit the *Xuanyi*.
By this analogy, we know that he did not re-edit it.

Sixth, regarding the commentary (*shuwen*), both the original edition and the revised edition were extant; however, this *Xuanyi* exists in only a single version, indicating that it was not subject to revision.
Seventh, regarding the seventh point: where the explanations in the sub-commentary (shu-wen) were deficient in their interpretation of the meaning, Jingxi privately added supplementary material.
Now that this work has been revised, why did he not compose a single chapter for those omissions that lacked explanation?
However, the meaning is not difficult to perceive; it is only feared that later students might engage in forced and erroneous interpretations, and thus I have offered this critique.
First, the title, in two parts:
first, the indication of the dharma.

Regarding the title *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning): the five chapters explain the title so exquisitely that they exhaustively capture the essential purport of the sutra; therefore, it is called *Xuanyi*.
2. Revealing the Agent.
"Śramaṇa" is translated here as "diligent cessation," meaning that through diligent effort one brings about the cessation and abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*).
The *Sūryodgama-sūtra* states: "One who quiets the mind and reaches the fundamental source is therefore called a śramaṇa."
"If one quiets the deluded mind of views and afflictions and realizes the fundamental source of the True Truth (paramārtha-satya), one is a śramaṇa of the Tripiṭaka and Shared Teachings.
If one quiets the deluded mind of the dust-like [afflictions] and realizes the fundamental source of the Conventional Truth (saṃvṛti-satya), one is a śramaṇa of the Distinct Teaching."
One who quiets the deluded mind of ignorance and realizes the fundamental source of the Middle Way is a Perfectly Integrated Śramaṇa.
Furthermore, one who sequentially quiets the three delusions and realizes the three fundamental natures is a Distinct Śramaṇa.
One who extinguishes the three delusions within a single mind is a Perfect (yuan) śramaṇa.
The present commentator of this commentary is such a person of the Perfect [Vehicle].
Furthermore, the term "śramaṇa" is applied across all teachings to encompass both cause and fruit.
Now, speaking from the perspective of the Master’s manifest traces, he was a śramaṇa within the causal stage prior to the [ten] abodes.
"Guanding" (Consecration) is his name;
it refers to a Bodhisattva at the rank of Consecration in the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), of the *Avataṃsaka*.
The Sūtra states: "Because the waters of the wisdom of all Buddhas are poured upon his crown, it is called 'receiving office' (śiṣyābhiṣeka); therefore, it is named 'Consecration' (abhiṣeka).
His name was Fayun (Cloud of Dharma), and his childhood name was Feifan (Not Ordinary).
This refers to a sage of the Ten Stages, not an ordinary person of the Three Grades of Worthies.
His secular surname was Wu; he was a native of Yixing in Changzhou. His ancestors had fled to Dong’ou and did not return, so he now resided in Zhang’an, Linhai.
His father died young, and his mother raised him.
When he was only three months old, she wished to give him a name; reflecting upon the categories of things, she did not yet know what title to apply.

At night, his mother recited the names of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; the child then imitated the sounds and phrases with clear articulation. Everyone was simultaneously struck with wonder, and they informed Huizheng of Shijing Temple.
Upon hearing this, the Dharma Master smiled and said,
"This child is no ordinary person.
He then gave him the name Fanbian (No Ordinary Person).

Upon reaching the age of seven, he returned to become a disciple of Master Zheng; his talents and learning flourished daily as he pursued both the profound mysteries of Buddhism and the Confucian classics. In his early twenties, he received full ordination and entered the monastic discipline.

By the time Master Zheng grew weary of the world and received the Way at Tiantai—specifically in the first year of the Zhide era of the Chen dynasty—he was twenty-seven years old by secular reckoning.

Zhiyi’s eloquence and talent moved like clouds and rained down like dew; of all those capable of receiving and memorizing his teachings, Master [Fazheng] alone was such a person. Thus, he gathered followers from every direction as a supreme general of the Dharma.
Later, in the tenth month of the tenth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he took up residence on the south side of Mount Tiantai and composed this commentary.
Five years later, he brought his pen to a close at Anzhou; this was the first year of the Wude era of the Tang dynasty.

He frequently lectured on this sutra at Shaojing Temple in Zhang’an; when he encountered pirates plundering the area, both monastics and laypeople rushed to take refuge with him, yet as he struck the bell to begin his lecture, his countenance showed no sign of fear.

The bandits raised their banners and headed toward the temple, but suddenly they beheld military standards that blazed like the sun; the men holding bows and grasping halberds stood over ten feet tall, fierce and spirited, causing the multitude of thieves to scatter in terror.
Such was the nature of his spiritual resonance and penetration.
His life story is recorded in the "Xi Chan" (Practitioners of Meditation) section of the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Xu Gaoseng Zhuan) of the Tang dynasty.
As for the auspicious signs accompanying the composition of his commentaries and the hardships he endured for the sake of the Dharma, these will be detailed in the following text.
He passed away at Guoqing Temple on the seventh day of the eighth month in the sixth year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, at the age of seventy-two.
At the time of his death, his body manifested slight illness, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room. He addressed his disciples, saying:
"The *Maitreya Sūtra* states: 'On the day the Buddha enters the city, the incense smoke is like clouds.'"
"Since you have burned much incense, I shall now depart.
He had a fellow student named Zhixi, whom the Master had personally ordained; Zhixi passed away in the first year of the Zhenguan era.
At the time of his death, he said:
"I am being born in Tuṣita Heaven.
I see the rows of jeweled seats of my former teacher, the Great Master Zhi, all occupied except for one seat, which is empty alone. He says:"
"Six years hence, the Dharma Master Guanding shall ascend this [throne] to preach the Dharma.
When he burned incense to verify his intention, it was clear that Maitreya had descended in spirit;
calculating the years and deliberating the timing, he confirmed that Xi’s words were not in error.
Therefore, regarding the title "Abhiṣeka" and the term "Dharmameghā," how could there be any fear of it exceeding the reality?
As for the word "compiled" (zhuàn), it means to collect together the words and meanings to provide an explanation.
Part Two of this text:
First, a general preface on the profound purport, in two sections;
first, the heading.

Regarding the title "Preface to the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra," this preface is specifically designated as the "Preface to the King" (*xuowang*) because it serves as the introductory exposition for the entire work; thus, it is distinguished by this specific label.
This is similar to how the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) separately designates its own preface to the sutra as the "Preface to the King."
To claim that this title should be deleted is incorrect.
Second, "Now, as for 'Correct'... and below, is the formal introduction, which has two parts:
first, a general praise of the ultimate convergence of the three virtues; second... [etc.]
First, praising the ultimate principle that is expressed, in three parts:

first, praising both phenomena and principle together, in two parts: first, directly praising the mutual fusion and identity of phenomena and principle; second, [praising their mutual inclusion]. (The first part: 1. Directly Praising the Mutual Fusion and Identity of Phenomena and Principle [End of section]
First, an eulogy on the principle inherent in phenomena;
second, an eulogy on the phenomena inherent in the principle.
The principle is that of the three thousand realms and the three truths, wherein the sentient and the Buddha are unified and cause and effect are without distinction.
"Phenomena" refers to the phenomena of delusion and enlightenment within the ten realms; they differ at their beginning and end, and are distinguished as new and old.
Nevertheless, when one realizes principle through phenomena, waves are nothing but water;
when one realizes phenomena through principle, water is nothing but waves.
Therefore, this principle is that which is elucidated by the present sutra; it is the ultimate goal of this teaching, and thus it is raised and extolled at the beginning of the text.
As for the initial phrase, "the true path" (*zhengdao*) refers to the wondrous principle; the phrasing is interwoven with ornamental elegance precisely to distinguish the true path from false paths.

In terms of its capacity for universal penetration, it refers to the principle of nirvāṇa and buddha-nature, which is free from the two extremes of deviation and universally penetrates all things; therefore, it is called the "Right Path.

As for its subtlety, it is neither vertical nor horizontal; its principle encompasses everything without exception, and being devoid of the clamor and movement of beginning or end, it is termed "Profound Stillness."
Because it is free from the obstructions of novelty and antiquity, it is called "void and profound" (*xūxuán*).
Furthermore, "mysterious stillness" (*yōujì*) refers to the wondrous principle being utterly transcendent; "void and profound" refers to the true path (*zhèngdào*) being empty and pervasive.
To speak of the true path as mysterious and still is because the true path is itself the wondrous principle.

That "the wondrous principle is void and profound" means that the wondrous principle is itself the True Path; thus, although there are two names, there is no duality of substance. Consequently, from the perspective of principle, there is no distinction between beginning and end, or new and old; yet from the perspective of phenomena, beginning and end, and new and old, are perfectly manifest.

Now, when we discuss principle, it is not separate from phenomena; it is such that within the beginning and end there is no beginning or end, and within the new and old there is no new or old—just as pointing to waves is itself pointing to water.
Second, from "without beginning" (*anādi*) onwards, there is praise for the phenomena that are identical with principle.
That which is without beginning or end possesses beginning and end; that which is without newness or antiquity possesses newness and antiquity—just as water is identical with waves.
When waves and water are fused into one, who can distinguish between principle and phenomenon?

Regarding "ignorance and birth-and-death being equal": ignorance is the beginning and end relative to the wisdom of all seeds, while birth-and-death is the beginning and end relative to nirvana; by overturning ignorance into the wisdom of all seeds, one realizes nirvana within birth-and-death.
"That which exists inherently" refers to the fact that one has been fundamentally deluded since beginningless time.
"Only through cultivating causes can it be realized" refers to attaining the fruits of wisdom and cessation by means of the conditions and the efficient cause.
Second, from the words "This sutra" onwards, [the passage] concludes that this is what is expounded in the present sutra.
Regarding the phrase "the beginning of what is not a beginning," the question is:
Previously, ignorance and birth-and-death were taken as the beginning; why is it now that the Buddha-nature and the three causes are taken as the beginning?
Answer: Ignorance and birth-and-death are, in essence, the three causes.
Second, from "If the Buddha... onwards, there is a detailed and further explanation in three parts:
First, the establishment of the premise.
The section beginning with "This is then" explains the meaning of the preceding two lines.
"Suchness" (*tathatā*) refers to both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*). Because the principle of the cause is identical to the principle of the fruit, Buddha-nature is not the cause.
1. "As for 'the fruit-as-such' (*yathā-phala*)," below this, the principle of the fruit is identical to the principle of the cause; therefore, *nirvāṇa* is not a fruit.
2. "If the cause... below this, is a re-explanation of the preceding passage.

Since it has been demonstrated that the principle of cause and effect is identical, it follows that not only is the principle realized by the ultimate fruit neither new nor old, but the principle possessed by ordinary beings at lower stages is likewise neither new nor old.

The text repeatedly explains and establishes this point, stating that "the suchness of the cause is not different from the suchness of the fruit, and the suchness of the fruit is not different from the suchness of the cause"; in essence, it merely reveals that the principle of cause and effect is one.
Question:
According to the previous explanation, *nirvāṇa* is taken as the "new" and *buddha-nature* as the "old.
In this context, it should have been stated that not only is the suchness (*tathatā*) of *nirvāṇa* not old, but why instead is it said to be not new?
Answer: If we clarify this in terms of cause and effect, it is indeed as you have questioned.
Although I have now analyzed the phrases to explain their meanings, I have merely demonstrated that the principles of cause and effect are identical; it is not that one is new and the other is old.
Therefore, the conclusion below states:
"Thus, the suchness of the Buddha-nature, nirvana, cause, and effect is neither new nor old.
Third, from "Thus" onwards, the conclusion is established.
3. Below the section "Not New," the text concludes by returning to the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
By correlating principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), the one nature and two cultivations together constitute the three virtues.
The one nature is the principle, which corresponds to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Although the principle fundamentally possesses all three, it is now treated as one in relation to cultivation.
Although both the cultivation of wisdom and the cultivation of abandonment are darkly merged with the principle, they are now treated as two in relation to the nature.
This combines nature into one and cultivation into two.

If explained by way of distinction, then both cultivation and nature each have three aspects: the principle encompasses the three bodies of the Dharmakāya; wisdom is the three types of Prajñā; and cessation is the three types of liberation.
Although the opening [of the ninefold categories] establishes nine, these nine are merely three; the three and the nine are mutually integrated, unfolding and interpenetrating without obstruction.
The following section clarifies that the essence, the doctrine, and the function each mutually contain the others; this is precisely that meaning.
Since understanding is established as being identical to principle, it is said to be "new without being new.
Since delusion is established as being identical to principle, it is said to be "old without being old.
Because delusion and understanding are both identical to principle, the wisdom of all modes does not arise, yet ignorance is severed without being severed.
Because it is three within one, it is not the verticality of a drop of water;
because it is one within three, it is not the horizontality of a blazing fire.
Neither vertical nor horizontal, it is like the letter "I" in its pristine form.

Generally speaking, the discussions regarding the cultivation and nature of practice—whether it progresses or not—are not uniform; the *Xianxing lu* (Record of Manifesting the Nature) elucidates this in full detail.
Second, the analysis of the origins of the expressive terminology has two parts:
first, a general overview of the entire dispensation.

Regarding the difference between the sharp and the dull: all sentient beings are fundamentally endowed with the three virtues, which are equal and without distinction; it is only due to the depth or shallowness of their habitual cultivation that the differentiation between the sharp and the dull arises.

Those of sharp faculties realize the perfect and eternal nature immediately upon sitting at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*; thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Upon first seeing my body and hearing what I have taught, they all believe and accept it, entering the wisdom of the Tathāgata."

Those of dull faculties are like the deaf or the mute; they remain entirely raw, like milk. Therefore, they must be gradually refined through the sequence of the three flavors, until they arrive at this present sutra, where they finally enter the secret treasury.

Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Except for those who have previously practiced and studied the Hīnayāna—such persons as these, I now likewise cause to hear this sūtra and enter the Buddha-wisdom."

Those with indeterminate faculties attain realization of the wondrous principle through the three samādhis; relative to those mentioned previously, they are termed "dull," while relative to those mentioned subsequently, they are termed "sharp.
Because these capacities are not uniform, there is a distinction among the teachings of the five periods; thus it is said, "Therefore, the Great Sage accords with conditions," and so forth.

"Sudden" refers to the *Avataṃsaka*, while "gradual" refers to the three periods of the Dharma-taste. The Deer Park is the beginning of the gradual; the Vaipulya is the middle of the gradual; and the Prajñāpāramitā is the end of the gradual. Before the assemblies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, both the sudden and the gradual are subsumed within that which is neither sudden nor gradual.
The phrase "As for 'sudden'" below serves to cite the subsequent scriptural passage as evidence to establish this meaning.
Regarding "the grass of patience" and so forth, the twenty-fifth [chapter] states: "In the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called 'Patience' (*kṣānti*)."
"If the ox eats it, it immediately obtains the *sarpis* (clarified butter).

Here, the Snowy Mountains are likened to the Buddha; the *kṣānti-grass* (patience-grass) is likened to the teaching; the ox is likened to the receptive capacity and conditions; eating is likened to practice; and obtaining is likened to entering the stage [of realization].

Those of sudden capacity strike upon the Buddha and hear the teaching of the Perfect and Sudden; hearing this teaching, they practice and attain realization, entering and abiding in the stages. This proves that those of sharp faculties awaken to the principle of the Three Virtues within the assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Although that [teaching] encompasses both the distinct and the universal, it is here explained primarily according to the Perfect [Teaching].

Regarding the phrase "As for the gradual," the thirteenth [chapter] states, "From the cow comes milk," which is a metaphor for the twelve divisions of the scriptures emerging from the Buddha—namely, the *Avataṃsaka*.
"From milk comes curd" is a metaphor for how from the twelve divisions [of the canon] come the nine divisions, namely the *Āgamas*.
"From curd comes fresh butter" is a metaphor for how from the nine divisions comes the *Vaipulya*.
“From fresh butter comes clarified butter” is a metaphor for how the *Prajñāpāramitā* emerges from the Vaipulya sutras.
“From clarified butter comes ghee” is a metaphor for how the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* emerges from the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
The *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* share the same purpose in revealing [the ultimate truth], and thus the latter is omitted here.
This serves as proof that [the audience] possesses dull faculties.

Since they were entirely like milk when [encountering] the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, they must pass through the three flavors in a gradual sequence to be refined and matured; only upon reaching the present sūtra do they finally awaken to the three virtues. Therefore, it is said that [the realization] is "gradually perfected."
Because one attains the perfection of the three virtues in this present sutra through the sequential order of the preceding four flavors, it is said that they are "perfected in succession.
Regarding the phrase "An analogy for this," the twenty-seventh [chapter] states: "If poison is placed in milk, the milk will kill a person immediately."
The same applies to placing poison in curd or the two types of clarified butter (*sarpis*):

"placing poison" refers to the manifesting cause (*vyākaraṇa-hetu*) of past habitual tendencies; however, the manifestation of that poison differs depending on whether one relies upon hearing the teachings now.

If one previously planted the seeds of the Perfect Vehicle (*paripūrṇa-yāna*) within the two types of clarified butter, then upon hearing [the teaching] again now, ignorance is immediately extinguished; this is called "killing the person."
This proof establishes that one may enter through the various flavors of the indeterminate faculties.
The phrase "all are" below serves as a summary.
Śākyamuni is translated here as Nengren (Capable Benevolence).

Those who profoundly exhaust the provisional and the real find that the increases and decreases across the five periods do not transcend the four teachings. What the various teachings expound—how could they ever depart from the ten realms?

The *Zang* and *Tong* teachings expound the six realms, while the *Bie* and *Yuan* teachings expound the ten; these four distinctions arise precisely because of the principles of identity and non-identity.

Now, the Tathāgata has fully revealed the principle that the ten realms are solely mind and that the nine provisional [realms] and the one real [realm] are equal in their provisional and real aspects; thus, it is said that he has "wondrously reached the ultimate.

Regarding the phrase "skillfully responding," this is also because sentient beings inherently possess both the provisional and the real, thereby eliciting the Tathāgata’s bestowal of provisional and real teachings.
Although the provisional and the real differ, their principle is eternally equal; thus, the *Famen pin* (Chapter on Non-duality) states:

"Because the capacities of sentient beings inherently possess that which is neither provisional nor real, they serve as the conditions for the provisional and the real; likewise, because the Buddha’s fruition inherently possesses that which is neither provisional nor real, he serves as the response for the provisional and the real."
"Qìng" means "exhausted.
"Shuǎng" means "lost.
Second, from "Now this" onwards, there is a separate clarification.
Regarding this sutra’s opening of the paths of the past and so forth: it opens the various provisional gates to reveal the true meaning of the present.
Thus, the *Lotus Sutra* says, "Opening the gate of expedient means, it reveals the true aspect."
Regarding "the secret meaning": if the Buddha had not spoken of it, those of the partial and small vehicles would not have known it; therefore, it is called the "secret meaning.

Furthermore, while previously he manifested expedient means, his underlying intent was directed toward the Perfect [Teaching]. Now that this intent is being discussed, it is said: "To manifest and reveal the Tathāgata’s secret meaning of expedient means."

Regarding those who ultimately do not enter *nirvāṇa*: those of the partial and limited vehicles believe that the Buddha is extinguished like ashes, whereas those of the perfect and sudden vehicle know that the Buddha is eternally abiding.
Second, from "This Sūtra" onwards, the five chapters of the profound meaning (*xuan-yi*) of the separate introduction (*bie-xu*).
First, the Introduction, in two parts:
First, the Extensive Introduction Explaining the Title, in two parts:
First, Translating the Name and Explaining its Meaning. Second, [the remaining part].
First, the explanation based on the three virtues, in two parts:
first, a general presentation of the Sanskrit text;
second, a word-by-word translation, in two parts:
First, the explanation of the individual names has three parts:
first, the opening of the chapters by way of translation and correspondence;
second, the formal explanation according to the chapters.

Regarding the two kinds of afflictions and birth-and-death: within the realm of desire, the afflictions of views and thought give rise to分段生死 (segmented birth-and-death); beyond the realm, the affliction of ignorance gives rise to 變易生死 (transformative birth-and-death).
Regarding "exempt from these causes and effects": "cause" refers to afflictions (*kleśa*), and "effect" refers to birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Below the section "General Explanation," it is called "Great" because it is pervasive and vast.
The three virtues (*tri-dharma*) are perfectly interfused and encompass the hundred realms; therefore, they all receive the name "Great."
Because they are perfectly interfused, both are free from the clamor and agitation of the two extremes, and thus are all termed "quiescent extinction" (śānti-nirvāṇa);
because they are perfectly interfused, both transcend the violent torrent of the two deaths, and thus are all named "ultimate."
III. From "The Distinctive and the Common" below, the intent is summarized to clarify the title.
"The unsurpassed, ultimate fruit" establishes the title by referring to the *nirvāṇa* manifested at the final stage of realization.
Second, the general designation.
Regarding the collective name for the sacred teachings, it is called "sūtra" because this term generally encompasses the Mahāyāna, Hīnayāna, partial, and perfect teachings.

As for its specific interpretation, as found in the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra), there are five meanings each for both the cases where a translation exists and where no translation exists.

Regarding the five meanings for which there is no equivalent translation: because those [Sanskrit] terms are rich in connotation while these [Chinese] terms are simple and shallow, it is impossible to translate a complex term with a simple one; thus, the original sound should be retained.
Since they cannot be translated, they contain five meanings:
first, the "source of phenomena" (*dharmatā*);...
2. Subtle Emission (also called Manifestation);
3. Gushing Spring; 4. Plumb Line.
Five. *Gandhavyūha* (Flower Garland).

There are five translations: first, translated as *sūtra*; second, translated as *yukti*; third, translated as *dharmamūla*; fourth, translated as "thread"; and fifth, translated as "well-spoken teaching."

In the past, when the Buddha-dharma was first transmitted and the relationship between Sanskrit and Chinese was not yet clear, there arose the theory that certain terms were "untranslatable. This view was propagated by the scholars of Hexi and has been inherited and employed by later generations.

Although the translators possessed all five qualifications, they took the *sūtra* as the primary standard; since the words of the ancient sages of this land were all termed *jing*, they accordingly designated the Buddha’s words as *jing*.
This meaning is the reverse [of that].

Therefore, within the Tripiṭaka there is only the Sūtra Piṭaka, and among the twelve divisions of scripture there is only the Sūtra division, without such names as the Vinaya Piṭaka or the Vinaya division.
2. From "If one possesses... onwards, the explanation is given in terms of the three truths (*trisatya*).

However, since the three virtues (*triguṇa*) and the three truths are identical in essence yet differ in name, the former [section] was explained by way of the three virtues, and the latter by way of the three truths.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, a re-translation of the specific names;
second, a further explanation of the three characters.
Initially, both the ultimate (paramārtha) and conventional (saṃvṛti) truths are termed "Great.

First, the ultimate truth is clarified: it is "great" because it universally dispels attachment to phenomenal characteristics; thus it is said, "It is as vast as empty space. Next, the conventional truth is clarified:
it is "great" because its essence fully possesses the three thousand realms; thus it is said, "Its nature is expansive and broad."
The subsequent name, "Middle Truth," is called "Great" because its negation and illumination are non-dual; thus it says, "it is also named 'inconceivable,' etc.
Regarding the phrase "not due to small characteristics": space is beyond all relativity; it is not named "great" in contrast to "small."
Second, it is called "extinction" (nirodha) in both the ultimate and conventional truths.
First, regarding the ultimate truth, it is called extinction in terms of one's own practice;
it is called extinction because it extinguishes the birth and death of ordinary beings.
The extinction of the twenty-five states of existence and the nirvana of the two vehicles is therefore called "as well as false and deceptive things.
Next, regarding the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it clarifies the extinction for the sake of transforming others:
by manifesting forms according to their respective categories, one extinguishes those three delusions; hence it is said that "one attains the twenty-five samādhis."
The twenty-five samādhis are as explained in the "Chapter on Noble Practices" (Śrī-vihāra-parivarta).

Subsequently, it clarifies that within the Middle Truth, both the cessation of the ultimate and the cessation of the conventional are extinguished; hence it says, "When birth and cessation have ceased."
Arising is the conventional (saṃvṛti) and cessation is the ultimate (paramārtha); since both extremes are extinguished, it is said that "having ceased.
This is the Middle Truth (madhyamā-satya), which is named the bliss of quiescent extinction (śānta-nirvāṇa).
Third, regarding why all three—ultimate, conventional, and middle—are termed "crossing" (tīraṇa): "crossing" takes the sense of transcending or surmounting.
The non-attachment to the three truths is entirely transcendent; all are thus given the name "crossing over.
Because one does not cling to the conventional, it is said that one crosses over what has not yet been crossed.
Because one does not cling to the ultimate truth, it is said that one further crosses over what has already been crossed.
The passage beginning with "Furthermore, crossing over this and that" explains crossing (*tāraṇa*) in terms of the Middle Truth (*madhyama-satya*).
It is called "crossing" because one does not cling to the simultaneous illumination (*dvaya-prakāśana*) of both.

Because one does not cling to the "other shore" of this and that through simultaneous negation (*dvaya-niṣedha*), it says, "one also crosses over what is neither that nor this," and so forth. Here, "this" refers to the conventional truth of saṃsāra, and "that" refers to the ultimate truth of nirvāṇa.
Regarding the divine tortoise (*shenguī*), the *Zhōnghuá gǔjīn zhù* states: "The numinous tortoise (*língguī*) possesses dark markings of five colors; it is the essence of the divine tortoise.
Its upper shell is convex, modeling the heavens, and its lower shell is flat, modeling the earth. It is able to perceive survival and ruin, and is clear-sighted regarding good and ill fortune."
"Crossing both water and land" is a metaphor for crossing over the two extremes via the Middle Way.
Water symbolizes birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), and land symbolizes nirvana.
Second, the summary.
Regarding the summary into the three dharmas, the "Chapter on Lamentation" states: "What is called the secret treasury?

It is like the three dots of the letter *i*; if they are placed side-by-side, they do not form an *i*, nor do they form one when placed vertically. Only when they are like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara does it become an *i*."

I am also like this: the dharma of liberation is not nirvāṇa, the body of the Tathāgata is not nirvāṇa, and mahāprajñā is also not nirvāṇa; nor is it nirvāṇa for these three dharmas to be distinct from one another.
Thus we know that being one yet three, and being three yet one, is precisely *nirvāṇa*.
Second, from "Vajra" onwards, there is a brief introduction to the remaining four [perfections].
However, the "Explanation of Names" provides a general discussion on the essence, substance, and function of the three dharmas, followed by a specific discussion of each of the three dharmas.

Since the general encompasses the specific and the specific does not depart from the general, the essence is itself the Great [Vehicle], the substance is itself the [Six] Perfections, and the function is itself Nirvana; these are merely the distinctions between the general and specific aspects of the three dharmas within the teachings. Therefore, the five chapters do not transcend these three dharmas.
Regarding "the Vajra-treasury" and so forth, the Twenty-one Sūtras state: "For example, a treasure-store contains many rare and extraordinary things, fully endowed with all varieties.
The profound and secret treasury of the Buddha-way is likewise; it contains many wonders, complete and without deficiency, and is named Great Nirvāṇa."

Because it does not perish through the two extremes, it is called "Vajra" (Diamond); because it encompasses the three thousandfold world-systems, it is named "Treasury of Jewels"; because there is no transition or change through the two types of death, it is called "Ever-Abiding"; because there is no burning affliction of the three delusions, it is called "Pure and Cool"; and being neither aging nor dying, it is the eternally abiding and unchanging.
Regarding "placing poison in the Buddha-nature": "poison" is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature, and the "five flavors" are a metaphor for the five destinies.
The Twenty-seventh Scripture states: "For example, if someone places poison in milk, even the *tīra* (clarified butter) will all become poisonous."
Although its name changes, the poisonous nature of the venom is not lost; even if one consumes clarified butter (*sarpirmaṇḍa*), it can still kill a person.
The Buddha-nature of sentient beings is likewise: although they dwell within the five destinies and receive diverse bodies, this Buddha-nature remains eternally one and unchanging.
One should understand that destroying delusions by means of seeing the nature is what is meant by "killing people"; this is precisely the powerful function of the present sutra.

The previous citation of the "poison-placed" analogy illustrated the teachings of the five periods; this citation of the "poison-placed" analogy illustrates how the capacities of beings across the five destinies are identical. Thus, while citing the same passage, the underlying intent in each case is distinct.
The "poisoned drum" is as described in the ninth sutra: "For example, suppose someone were to smear a new drum with poison and strike it among a crowd of people.
Although they have no intention of hearing it, those who hear it will all die, with the sole exception of those whose deaths are not untimely."
This sutra is likewise: among the multitude of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), for those who hear its sound, all three poisons are entirely extinguished.

Although there may be no intentional thought, by the power of this sutra, it can extinguish afflictions, grave offenses, and the commission of the five rebellious acts (*ānantarya*). Having heard it, one also creates the causal conditions for Bodhi and gradually severs the afflictions—excepting only those of the *icchantikas* who meet with untimely deaths.
Regarding the eight masteries (*vaśitā*): first, mastery over unity and multiplicity.
He manifests a single body as many bodies, with the number and size of these bodies filling the ten directions like motes of dust.
The body of the Tathāgata is in truth not composed of atoms, yet because of his sovereign mastery, he manifests a body of minute atoms.
Second, regarding size:
he displays a body the size of a single atom filling the great trichiliocosm.
3. Lightness and heaviness:
Although one may lift a body as vast as the great trichiliocosm and fly through the air, in reality there is neither lightness nor heaviness. 4. Form and mind.
The Tathāgata dwells with single-minded composure and immovability, yet manifests and transforms into immeasurable forms and categories.
Five: the faculties. Six:
the mutual functioning of the six sense-faculties.
Sixth, attainment:
attaining all dharmas, yet without the notion of attainment.
Seventh, teaching.
If one were to recite a single verse for immeasurable eons, its meaning would still not be exhausted.
Eighth, regarding "vision":
the Tathāgata pervades all places; like space, he cannot be seen. This is as explained in detail in the twenty-first sūtra.

Regarding the two characters for "eternal abiding" (*nitya-vasthita*), the "Chapter on Life Span" states: "One should always bind the mind to the practice of these two characters; the Buddha is eternally abiding.
If there are those who cultivate these two characters, you should know that such persons follow my practice and will reach the place where I have reached."
The "Chapter on the Four Truths" states: "If one hears even the two characters 'eternally abiding' (nitya), and they but once pass through the ear, one will immediately be reborn in the heavens.

As for the "unsurpassed ghee" (paramā-mṛdvīkā), it refers to what the sutra says: "Just as ghee is produced from matured butter, so too is the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* produced from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*."
Second, the section beginning with "The title contains" concludes [the discussion].

Regarding "the characteristics of the ultimate teaching": the words spoken by the Sage for the sake of those below are called "teaching" (jiao), while the differentiation of their similarities and differences is called "characteristics" (xiang).
This means that the three virtues (triguṇa) of this present sutra are perfectly interfused, differing from the partial and inferior teachings which are either vertical or horizontal.
Furthermore, when compared with the preceding sections, although the clarity and perfection are the same, they differ in their inclusion and equality.
Although they have now received the profound gift of equally knowing the Buddha-nature, their status remains equal; yet the underlying principles are eternally distinct.
Regarding the five different regions of India, all five nations are called "Tianzhu" (India), yet their spoken languages differ from one another.
"India" is sometimes called Shendu or Xian-dou, both of which are corruptions. The correct term is Indu;
"Indu" is a name for the moon, and as the moon has a thousand names, this is one such appellation.
It is truly because the worthy and sages of that land have succeeded one another, enlightening all living beings and illuminating them like the moon; it is for this reason that it is so named.

As for the slight difference between "shē" (奢) and "qiè" (切), it means that while their spoken sounds are largely the same, they differ only slightly in that the former is more relaxed and the latter is more intimate.

Just as what is called *mahā* in the Central Kingdom is referred to as *maheśvara* in the Southeast, so too do the dialects here differ greatly in pronunciation; for instance, what is called *parinirvāṇa* in the Central Kingdom is called *nirvāṇa* in the Northwest.
The region south of the Huai River is called Chu, while the Central Plains are called Xia; Chu is thus a land of the "barbarians" (man-yi).
The language of the Central Plains is standard, resembling that of the Middle Kingdom;
the speech of the Huai and Chu regions is corrupt, resembling that of the northwest.
The *Chunqiu Houguyu* states: "The descendant of Ji Lian, the ancestor of Chu, was named Zhuyong. His son served King Wen of Zhou and died young.
His son was Xiong Ren; Ren begot Xiong Yi, whom King Cheng enfeoffed in the region of the Chu barbarians in recognition of the labors of Kings Wen and Wu."
Kong Anguo said: "A large state is called Xia.
As for the "Double Scroll," it contains two distinct scriptures within itself.

The first was preached at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha and is titled the *Buddhaparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, consisting of two volumes, upper and lower; it was translated by Bó Fǎzǔ during the Western Jin dynasty.

The first was preached in the Mahāvana (Great Forest) of the Vaisālī kingdom at the multi-storied lecture hall; it is titled the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* and consists of two volumes, upper and lower, translated by the Eastern Jin monk Faxian.
Both of these two versions belong to the Hīnayāna.
The six-fascicle version, titled the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, was also translated by Faxian.
As for the "Great Version," it refers to the six-fascicle text translated by Dharmakṣema; this is merely the preliminary section of the Great Version.
The section below this [heading] refutes past errors.

In the *Zhao lun* (Treatise by Sengzhao), the *Niepan wuming lun* (Treatise on the Namelessness of Nirvana) states: "Nirvāṇa, nīrvāṇa, and nibbāna—these three names appeared at different times; they are likely merely variations between the dialects of Chu and Xia, with 'nirvāṇa' being the correct form."
Therefore, it is now stated that this is the correct phonetic transcription for that land.
Regarding the phrase "as for saying 'great'": since the term "great" in this region encompasses many meanings, it serves as an analogy for why *nirvāṇa* is not translated unilaterally.
That all things reach this state is itself nirvāṇa.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Among all dharmas, nirvāṇa is the foremost.
Furthermore, in the chapter on "The Merits of Names" (*Nāmaguṇa-parivarta*), it says: "That which is called 'Great' is termed 'Eternal' (*nitya*)."
Regarding "supernatural powers" (*abhijñā*), the *Ratnavyūha Sūtra* states: "The name 'divine' (*shen*) refers to the celestial mind, and 'penetration' (*tong*) refers to the nature of wisdom.
When the celestial mind and the nature of wisdom are fully developed to their ultimate limit, they are termed "great"; hence it is called the "Supreme Title."
Below the term "constant bliss" (nitya-sukha), it is called "great" because it collectively encompasses the four virtues; thus, it is termed a "comprehensive name.
Therefore, it cannot be translated, as *nirvāṇa* contains many meanings, and thus the Sanskrit term is retained.
Regarding these phenomena of form and sound: because they are written by hand, they belong to form; because they are spoken by mouth, they belong to sound.
From the word "cannot" (*buké*) onwards, [the text] repeatedly writes of this form and repeatedly speaks of this sound.
The intention is this:
since the Sanskrit name has already been written, it is not permissible to write the Chinese name again.
Furthermore, a single Sanskrit name may encompass many meanings; since these cannot be explained exhaustively, it is for this reason that the term is not translated.
Regarding the phrase "how could meanings be many?": this master does not allow that a single name can contain multiple meanings.
The section beginning with "But only one" correctly demonstrates his own position, again citing the character *xi* (rest) from this region as an example.
Question:
Are the meanings of "much" (*bahu*) and "many" (*prabhūta*) not the same? Answer:
They are not the same. For instance, when instructing one's children, there is only the single meaning of "child"; thus, beneath the name "child," there are no further multiple meanings.
These views held by human teachers are merely products of their own subjective perceptions and are certainly not universal.
In some cases, "long breath" (*cháng xī*) is explained by taking *shēng zhǎng* (to grow and develop) as the meaning of *xī*.
"Temporary news" (*zànshí xiāoxī*) takes cultivation and nourishment as the meaning of *xiāoxī*.
"Informing of news" (*bàoshì xiāoxī*) takes sound and message as the meaning of *xiāoxī*.
Regarding "one name with four realities": *Sindhava* is a single name that possesses four realities—salt, a vessel, water, and a horse.
As for the wise minister who understands this well, the "Bodhisattva Chapter" states: "In this way, these four things share a common name; a wise minister thoroughly understands this name."

If the king seeks *saindhava* while bathing, one immediately presents water; if the king seeks *saindhava* while eating, one immediately presents salt; if he wishes to drink, one presents a vessel; if he wishes to travel, one presents a horse.
The sūtra uses this as a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s esoteric teachings, which only the wise ministers of the Mahāyāna should be able to understand thoroughly.
The "four equanimities" refer to loving-kindness (maitrī), compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekṣā).
They are also called the "four immeasurables" (catvāry apramāṇāni); the term "immeasurable" derives from the object, while "four equanimities" derives from the mind.
Although objects of perception are infinite, my mind remains ever-equal.
To "replace the heavy with the light" means to substitute *prajñā* (wisdom) for *paññā* (insight).
As for "Zhendan," it is also called Zhendan, Chandan, Zhina, or Zhinan; these are all variations resulting from the phonetic shifts of the Sanskrit sound.
If one follows the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it is translated as "Han Land.
Furthermore, in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, there are two pronunciations:
the first is *zhina* (指那), which means "land of culture and refinement" (*wénwù guó*). This praises this region as a land of robes, caps, and refined culture.
The second term, *yunzhi* (雲指), means "difficult to reach"; here it is translated as "frontier regions," thereby disparaging this land as not being the Central Kingdom (*madhyadeśa*).
The *Record of the Western Regions* (*Xiyuji*) translates *Mahācīna* as the "Great Han Country."
Some claim that because the sun rises from the eastern corner with a color like vermilion, it is called Zhendan or Zhendan; these are all errors.
"Zhu Daosheng" consists of "Zhu," which is his surname, and "Daosheng," which is his given name.
His original surname was Wei, and he was a native of Julu. From childhood, he was exceptionally perceptive; his intelligence and wisdom were as if divine.
Later, meeting the śramaṇa Zhu Fatai, he renounced his secular life to receive instruction from him, and consequently adopted the surname Zhu.

Regarding the noble one named Nianbo: he was born in Chang’an during the early years of the dynasty and studied the Dharma under Kumārajīva; the monastic community of Guanzhong all regarded him as possessing divine insight.
Later, he returned to Jiankang and resided at Qingyuan Temple. This temple was so named because it was the site where Lady Chu, the Empress Gongsi of the Jin dynasty, had grown green vegetables.

As the six-fascicle *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* first arrived at the capital, Daosheng analyzed its principles and penetrated its subtle depths; he then asserted that even icchantikas could attain Buddhahood and subsequently composed fourteen topical treatises.

Regarding the meaning of the tenth category of sentient beings possessing Buddha-nature, it says: "When the sutra states that icchantikas lack [Buddha-nature], this is intended to exhort those who commit evil deeds; it does not mean they truly lack it."
Because he perceived that evil is empty and non-existent, while the absence of evil necessarily implies its existence, his exaltation and disparagement were suited to the occasion.
How could one who discerns the subtle essence of things merely cling to the literal text?
At that time, the Great Text had not yet been transmitted; his solitary insight arose first, and his unique vision offended the multitude.

Thereupon, those of the old school regarded this as heterodox teaching, and their censure and indignation grew ever more intense; they eventually brought it before the great assembly and expelled him.
Standing in the midst of the assembly, he assumed a solemn countenance and vowed:
"If what I have spoken contradicts the meaning of the scriptures, may I manifest a loathsome disease in this very life."
"If my words do not contradict the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), I pray that when the time comes for me to relinquish my life, I may sit upon the lion throne.
Having finished speaking, he brushed his robes and departed.
He first went to Mount Huqiu in Wu, where within ten days several hundred disciples gathered to study under him.

In the summer of that year, thunder struck the Buddha hall at Qingyuan Temple, and a dragon ascended into the heavens, leaving its radiance upon the western wall; consequently, the name of the temple was changed to Longguang (Dragon Radiance).
Contemporaries sighed and said:
"Now that the dragon has departed, the Master’s life must surely come to an end."
Shortly thereafter, he set out for Mount Lu, where he withdrew his presence among the mountain crags; the entire monastic community came to revere and submit to him.

Later, when the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* reached the Southern Capital, it indeed proclaimed that even icchantikas possess Buddha-nature, which accorded with what [Huiyuan] had previously stated as if two pieces of a tally fit together.

Having obtained this sutra, he immediately began to lecture upon it. On the day of Gengzi, the eleventh month of winter in the eleventh year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he ascended the Dharma seat at the Lingyan Monastery on Mount Lu; his countenance was radiant and clear, and his sublime voice resonated with great power.
After several rounds of debate, they exhausted all principles and reached the ultimate subtlety; among those present to observe and listen, there was none who was not enlightened and delighted.

As the dharma assembly was about to conclude, he suddenly saw his fly-whisk fall in a flurry. He sat upright with a composed countenance, leaning on his armrest, and passed away; his facial expression did not change, appearing as if he had entered meditative absorption.
Thereupon, the monks of the capital felt inward shame and self-reproach, and they pursued him with faith and submission.
This man’s insight was so profound that the auspicious signs manifested were as such.
He once composed the *Nirvāṇa-jì*, the details of which are recorded exhaustively in the ninth fascicle of the *Liang Zhuan*.
Because his vision regarding *nirvāṇa* was uniquely like this, the people of the time praised him as a sage.
The phrase "below" refers to the passage citing the chanting of "extinction, swift extinction," which indicates that the translator rendered *nirvāṇa* as "extinction."
"Under 'the former school,' this is the current Master’s judgment.

'The former' refers to Master Daosheng; 'the latter' points to the Zangyan [school], which asserts that extinction occurs swiftly. However, because they refer only to the physical body (*janmakāya*), they speak of it as merely ceasing."
Regarding "arising and then ceasing," that which ceases is also the cessation of *nirvāṇa*.
Because both extremes are extinguished, it is called "quiescent extinction" (*śānti-nirodha*).
Baima cites the second passage, Changgan cites the fifteenth passage, and Dinglin cites the fifth passage.
"Ulcers and warts" refers to the two types of death.

Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty cited twenty-three scriptural passages: in the causal stage, the application of wisdom is called "severance," while in the resultant stage, the exhaustion of delusions is called "non-arising."
Below the heading "Master E" (Eishi) is the preface to Master E’s commentary on the treatise.

Regarding the term "the Qin language": among the various Qin dynasties—namely the Qin of the fall of the Han (Wang Qin), Fu Qin, Yao Qin, and Qifu Qin—"Qin" here refers to Yao Qin, also known as De Qin; Fu Qin is referred to as Former Qin.
Rui was a disciple of Master Kumārajīva, belonging to the era of the Yao Qin dynasty.
"Tabular volumes" (fāngcè) refers to the scriptures and records of this land.

The "Zhōngyōng" chapter of the *Lǐjì* states: "The governance of Wén and Wǔ is spread throughout tabular volumes," and Zhèng Xuán’s commentary explains: "'Fāng' means tablets; [the 'cè' means slips]."
"Chè (a fascicle) means a slip of bamboo. Some say:
"A single strip is called a jiǎn (slip); several slips bound together are called a chè (fascicle)."
Thus, the "Preface to the Zuo Zhuan" states: "Major matters are recorded on bamboo slips; minor matters are merely noted on wooden tablets.
That which cannot be changed in its Sanskrit pronunciation refers to that which cannot be translated.
The Tripitaka Master of the Tang clearly stated that there are five instances where a term must not be translated:
first, the esoteric, such as *dhāraṇī*;
second, the polysemous, such as *bhagavat*.
Third, that which does not exist in this land, such as the Jambu tree;
fourth, that which accords with antiquity, such as Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
fifth, that which generates goodness, such as Prajñā.
The term "Nirvana" (涅槃) is not translated here; it should follow the precedent of retaining foreign terms when they serve to generate wholesome qualities or contain multiple meanings.
The phrase "immediately recorded it" (即時書之) uses "ji" (即), meaning "in regard to" or "at that very moment.
"Jiang" (匠) refers to a master artisan; here, it refers to the Master [Kumārajīva].
"Recipient" (*shòu zhě*) refers to the scribe, meaning the person who received the dictation.
"Jin" (謹) means reverence.
The phrase "As for the 'Four Clouds'... and below, because the principle being expounded is inconceivable, it is expressed as a double negation using neither Chinese nor Sanskrit terms.
Furthermore, because the principle is inconceivable, it cannot be translated [into Chinese].
However, *mahā* can indeed be translated as "great," so it is not the case that it is untranslatable.

Regarding the phrase "the basis of cessation" (*nirodha-adhiṣṭhāna*) below: "dharmas" refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and "person" (*pudgala*) refers to a conventional designation (*prajñapti*).
Below the term "birth and death" (*saṃsāra*), one extinguishes the deluded phenomena of birth and death and realizes the true phenomenon of *nirvāṇa*.

One transforms from a person who is a cause for ordinary beings into a person who has attained the fruit of ultimate sainthood; this explains the meaning of "deliverance" (*tāraṇa*) through transformation.

Regarding the statement that "extinction" (nirodha) refers to "non-existence," "refers to" means "titles. One titles non-existence with the term "extinction," and one titles existence with the term "crossing over" (tāraṇa).
Since both the substantial dharma and the provisional person—along with the five aggregates—are unobtainable, it is said that they are both extinguished.

The continuity [of existence] is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); because one proceeds from cause to fruit and transforms the state of an ordinary person into that of a sage, both [the body and the afflictions] are transcended.

Regarding the phrase "Thirdly," suffering based on the physical body is called *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder), while the simultaneous extinction of both body and wisdom is called *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder).
That which is not eternally exempt refers to one who, after death, is born again; therefore, it is merely called "extinction.
Only when the Buddha no longer undergoes birth within the three realms can he be said to have attained "crossing over" (nirvāṇa).
The section beginning with “The Master Guān” critiques the initial interpretation of Kāishān.

Regarding the question of upon what basis those in the cycle of birth and death are delivered: how could persons and dharmas ever be separated? Since the provisional person of a sentient being exists based on the real dharmas of the five aggregates—just as a fist is formed by grasping fingers—they do not possess distinct essences.
"Since that dharma has already been extinguished first, upon what can that person rely for deliverance?
This objection clarifies the meaning of "extinction.

Regarding the phrase "If [the person] is born," since the person can undergo transformation, one may infer by analogy that the dharma can also undergo transformation; because there is no distinct essence between the person and the dharma, how can it be said that the dharma of birth and death is extinguished?
This objection challenges the explanation of the meaning of "crossing over" (*tāraṇa*).
From the words "Now, investigating... onwards, the Master [Hui-kuang] examines it through the lens of the four teachings, sequentially refuting those four interpretations.

Regarding the statement that "the birth-and-death of the three fruits has not yet been entirely extinguished": although the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) has extinguished the birth-and-death of the four miserable realms, they still undergo seven births among humans and devas in the desire realm; the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*) still has one birth remaining.

Although the three fruits [of stream-enterer, once-returner, and non-returner] lack the cycle of birth and death in the desire realm, they still possess the cycles of birth and death in the form and formless realms; therefore, these first three fruits have not yet completely extinguished [all existence].
The section beginning with "All phenomena" below raises an objection based on liberation with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-vimukti*).
The severance of the fetters of the "son" is called the cessation of the cause; the persistence of the body as the basis for suffering is called the non-cessation of the effect.

Regarding the phrase "If [it were] ashes," etc., this addresses the objection concerning the simultaneous quiescence of both the provisional person and the provisional dharmas in the state of *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder); that is to say, the provisional person and the precious dharmas.
"If one is in quiescence, there is no discussion of 'crossing over'. Since the person has already attained quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*), with reference to whom could one discuss crossing over?

"Furthermore, below" refers to the fact that what is discussed in the Lesser Teachings (*hīnayāna*) is that the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) attain realization in the remainderless state (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), and thus there is no principle of becoming a Buddha.

Regarding the statement that "all phenomena are neither extinguished nor otherwise," because the Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka do not sever their afflictions, the question of whether they are extinguished or not is not raised.

As for "crossed over" or "not crossed over," this is because [phenomena] are fundamentally unborn and thus now have no extinction; both phenomena and persons are alike like illusions and transformations.
The phrase "not only" [indicates that] the extinction of false dharmas occurs in the Ten Abodes, while the extinction of true dharmas occurs in the Ten Practices.
Because false dharmas are extinguished, ordinary people are delivered; because [the attachment to] nirvana is extinguished, sages are delivered.
Regarding the statement that "it does not involve the true Dharma," this explains that [the term] *nirodha* (extinction) merely refers to the extinction of the phenomena of birth and death.

In the phrase "the words do not... and below, it explains that *tāraṇa* (deliverance) merely refers to the transformation of the person within birth and death; therefore, it is said that it does not involve the truth and does not concern the sages.

Regarding "extinction" (nirodha) and "crossing over" (pāramitā) as neither vertical nor horizontal: extinction refers to the three gates of liberation, while crossing over refers to the three types of prajñā. Although their substance is identical while their names differ, the triad and the unity are mutually identical, thus being neither vertical nor horizontal.

Regarding the phrase "neither... nor": "Small" refers to the Tripiṭaka (Śrāvaka) teaching; "Common" refers to the Shared (Pratyekabuddha) teaching; "Bodhisattva" refers to the Distinct teaching; and "Buddha" refers to the Perfect teaching. These four teachings alone constitute the Dharma-words of the former sages.
Since both [existence and non-existence] are not [ultimately real], I do not dare to speak of them.

As for the statement that "experiencing this existence or non-existence is still suffering" and so forth: because one experiences these two views, there is oppression, which constitutes suffering (*duḥkha*); because one clings to these and gives rise to delusion, it becomes the origin (*samudaya*); because one practices their antidotes, it is the path (*mārga*); and because one is free from both permanence and annihilation, it is cessation (*nirodha*).
This refutes the doctrine of existence and non-existence held by the Kaishan school as being entirely identical to the views of annihilationism and eternalism.

As for the statement "it is still the Truth of Cessation," this means that even if one were to eliminate annihilationism and eternalism, one would still not have transcended the Tripitaka of the Hinayana; since one’s intent has not yet reached the Mahayana, it is said to be "still" [the Truth of Cessation].

Regarding the phrase "the truth of the cessation [of suffering]," what is taught by Kaishan does not even accord with the meaning of cessation in the Hinayana; how, then, could it explain the present Perfect and Sudden (yuantun) nirvana?
If one takes this to mean "that which exists," it merely restates the general principle.
"Regarding 'If both' and below," press and fix both eyes.
"As for 'birth and death,'" this means that both nirvāṇa and saṃsāra are discussed in relation to birth and death.
"Regarding 'Birth and death are fundamentally... and below, this constitutes the formal objection.

Regarding the phrase "there is no one who attains the Dharma," since real dharmas do not exist, the provisional person likewise does not exist; therefore, it is said that there is "no one who attains.
The section beginning with "Since it is impossible" [refers to] the fact that birth and death are fundamentally empty, like illusions and transformations.
Regarding the passage beginning with "How much less," it means that even saṃsāra is not permissible, let alone nirvāṇa. As for the term *wò-zhuì* (疣贅):
the first character is pronounced *yóu* (尤), and the second is pronounced by the phonetic *zhī* (之) and the rhyming suffix *ruì* (汭).
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Wou (疣) means a fleshy excrescence.

The *Shiming* says: "'Wou' refers to a mound (*qiu*)."
"Emerging from the skin is like a mound upon the earth.

The passage beginning with "If one... refutes [the view] according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao).
For now, it takes the Middle Way of the first stage (*bhūmi*) as *nirvāṇa*.
In the text, the heterodox views are addressed first, followed by the Small Vehicle; this sequentially grants concessions to both extremes before refuting them.
Even if it is not a false attachment, it is still a limited meaning; even if it is not a limited meaning, it is still a path of teaching. These two extremes are certainly not the Middle Way.

Regarding the statement that "Nirvana summons dharmas by name" and so forth: this means that the name "extinction" (nirvāṇa) summons both existent and non-existent dharmas, and these existent and non-existent dharmas correspond to the name "extinction."
Regarding the phrase "where names and things still persist," "things" refers to dharmas.
As for "that which can penetrate the crude": this is crude because it relies on the Tripitaka and the Two Vehicles to perform the analytical deconstruction of form (*rūpa*).
Regarding "that which penetrates the false": this refers to the partial truth realized, which is not ultimate reality.
Those who dwell in the city of transformation while in poverty lack the wealth and provisions of the Mahāyāna, just as a poor man dwells in a thatched hut.
Their distress at the long distance of the Buddha-way is like a weary merchant seeking temporary rest in a city of transformation.

The *Lotus Sūtra* reveals and clarifies [the truth], shattering the stagnant attachments of the "grass hut" and sweeping away the dogmatic adherence to the "transformed city"; therefore, it is said that [these former teachings] have long been discarded.

Regarding the phrase "How could," [the author asks]: how can one employ the meanings already discarded by the *Lotus Sūtra* to explain the name of the perfect and eternal [teaching] of the present sūtra?
Regarding the two extremes of partiality and deviation: in view of the principle of the "Middle Only" (but-chung) within this specific teaching, both extremes are entirely partial and deviant.
As for "existence not being related to non-existence," etc.: because existence and non-existence are not integrated, this is not the meaning of the Perfect (yuan).
"Running amok and left in disarray" means that each follows their own nature, thus they are "longitudinal," and together they attain their state, thus they are "transverse.
Regarding "plundering" (jié luó) below: "luó" (掠) is pronounced with the initial *l* and the final *shàng-fǎn* (a retroflex nasal); it means to seize or take away by force.
The sutra uses the analogy of non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) stealing the Buddha’s names of "permanence" and "bliss," comparing them to plundering a herd of oxen.
Now, [the text] rebukes Kaishan for merely seizing the name of "nirvana" (nirodha), which is like raiding a herd of oxen.
Not knowing its meaning is like failing to understand how to drill and rotate [a fire-drill].

Even the "milk-curd" (kṣīra) and "whey" (maṇḍa) of the Tripiṭaka are still difficult to obtain; how much more so the two types of "butter"—the Shared and the Distinct—and the "ghee" (ghṛta) of the Perfect [Teaching]?
Furthermore, the extinction of ignorance is not yet ultimate because it involves the partial realization of true suchness through the destruction of ignorance.

If the characters "extinction and liberation" (mièdù) appear above the word "only then" (fāngdé), it is a textual error. Regarding the phrase "from hereafter" (yǐhòu):

Furthermore, it would follow that an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) who merely goes from here to there would be one who has "crossed over" (tīrṇa). In the initial objection of the text regarding ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and their successive, overlapping states, the intention is as follows:
"If it is admitted that these are 'extinguished' (*nirodha*), they must therefore be 'crossed over' (*tīrṇa*);

How can it be said that "extinction" (nirodha) applies to ordinary persons (pṛthagjana), while "crossing over" (tāraṇa) applies only to noble ones (ārya)?

Regarding the passage beginning with "If [they were] noble," the following objection is raised: since it is granted that the meaning of extinction for noble ones is the same as for ordinary persons, by analogy, the meaning of crossing over should likewise be the same; therefore, it says, "Noble ones go from here to there," and so forth.
The phrase "If they were the same" and below concludes the objection.
If they were the same as ordinary beings and sages in the Hinayana, then they would approximate the limited fruits of the Lesser Vehicle rather than reaching the height of ultimate perfection;
they would be narrow, encompassing only the six realms of existence, rather than being broad enough to include the ten realms.

The section beginning with "If it were different" [states that] even if it were distinct from ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and sages, it would merely be a case of the general and the particular; therefore, it would likewise not be lofty or vast.
The section beginning with "How could it be" concludes by means of a refutation.

Regarding the statement that "one should formulate sixteen variations by four times four," this refers to challenging the third and fourth interpretations; one should likewise apply the same pattern as for the first two interpretations to challenge them with the four teachings, thus resulting in sixteen.

Now, the extant text is abbreviated; the first two interpretations each apply to the four teachings, thus forming eight, while the latter two interpretations are each combined into one, resulting in only ten sections.
Nevertheless, although the text of the latter two interpretations consists of only one section each, their meanings respectively encompass all four teachings.
The third [point], by means of the distinction between *śeṣa* (with remainder) and *nir-śeṣa* (without remainder), as well as the three delusions, already encompasses the four teachings.

Since the fourth [point] refutes [the other teachings] on the grounds that they are proximate and narrow rather than lofty and vast, it follows that the lofty and vast must belong to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).
The three [categories] of "proximate," "narrow," and "comprehensive" each contain four meanings; their purport is as clear as day.
Under the heading "Luminous Wisdom," the intention behind the inclusion and omission is shown.
"Zhe" (哲) means wisdom (*jñāna*).
The section beginning with “People of the time” below demonstrates the intent of the critical inquiry.
*Lǚ* (薳) is pronounced *wěi*, meaning "distant.

This section is divided into two parts:
first, an explanation is provided by temporarily resorting to a sequential and individual analysis; second... [the remainder of the text follows].
Next, this section specifically addresses the principle of perfect interpenetration (*yuanrong*) in order to reveal the ultimate truth.

Without the preceding stage of distinct enumeration, there would be no means to reveal the subsequent perfect interpenetration; and without the subsequent perfect interpenetration, there would be no means to unify the preceding distinct enumeration. Therefore, one should know that perfect interpenetration is not a separate dharma at all, but is simply the realization that the three sets of nine [categories] mutually encompass one another.

Furthermore, both passages interrogate the teaching on the secret treasury found below in the "Chapter on Lamentation" (Sokavarga) to clarify its meaning; within the sequential exposition, they cite the passage on the Dharma-teaching to conclude the discussion on the three bodies. Thus it is said that the "secret treasury" is named Mahāparinirvāṇa. The three dots of the letter *i* and the three eyes of Śiva are merely metaphorical explanations, serving as analogies for the three virtues (*triguṇa*); therefore, there is no separate path.

Now, for the sake of convenience in explaining the meaning, the phrase "this written word" (*idaṃ vyañjanam*) should be used to conclude the section on *vimokṣa*; "the eye can illuminate and perceive" should be used to conclude the section on *prajñā*. Upon reaching the explanation of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), one takes the text of the combined analogy to conclude its meaning; therefore, it says, "The Dharma-body is also not [existent]," and so forth.

Therefore, regarding the secret treasury discussed in the "Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra" (The Lotus Sutra), the three meanings of the Dharma, the parable, and their synthesis do not diverge in their ultimate intent.

Since the Dharma and the parable are used to demonstrate the distinct stages [of the teaching], while the synthesis of the texts demonstrates their perfect fusion, one knows that the meaning of these two passages converges upon a single principle.

Below the phrase "unperceivable," he rebukes [the opponent] by stating that this is not yet the primary intent of the present sutra, and thus one must abandon the sequential and distinct to seek the perfectly integrated.
From "If one attains this meaning" onwards, he explains that throughout the sutra, there are many instances where the distinct is employed for the sake of the perfectly integrated.
"Excellently emerging" (*xiùchū*) means that excellence also emerges; it also signifies flourishing.

Regarding "the correspondence of the illumination and manifestation of the realm of wisdom": wisdom illuminates the realm, and through the realm, wisdom is manifested. Because the realm is great and wisdom is great, it is called "correspondence."
The object is the *dharmakāya*, and the wisdom is the *saṃbhogakāya*.
As for the sovereignity of the *nirmāṇakāya*, it pervades the entire *dharmadhātu* like images appearing in a mirror.
Since forms appear in response to objects, it is said that nothing can obstruct or sever it.
Regarding "neither born nor arisen": what arises previously is the cause, and what arises subsequently is the effect.
From "illuminating non-existence" onwards, the text explains its meaning of "perfection" (*yuan*) by means of "pervasiveness" and "sufficiency."
"Shining everywhere without exception" means that the perfect cessation is all-pervasive, as it illuminates the three truths.
"Arising without deficiency" means that the essential cessation is fully endowed, as it gives rise to the three wisdoms.
Although both object and wisdom are mentioned together, this primarily reveals that the retributive wisdom (vipākajñāna) has reached perfect cessation.
Because its illumination is all-pervasive, its clarity is ultimate; because it has set forth its course, its engagement with objects is final.

Regarding "meeting those who must be met": by employing the four methods of teaching to meet the capacities for the provisional and the real, and by manifesting birth and extinction for both oneself and others, one accords perfectly with the capacities of beings without contradiction; thus, it is called "meeting those who must be met."
"Taking what must be mastered" has the same meaning as the preceding phrase;
"mastering" (kè) means to overcome.
Regarding "the teacher of all Buddhas": the Buddhas are wisdom, and the teacher is the objective realm.
Because the objective realm can give rise to wisdom, it is called the Teacher of the Buddha.

It is not this shore of non-quintessence, nor that shore of ultimate realization, nor the middle current of partial truth; it is neither the wisdom that accords with reality nor the principle that is accorded with; it is a cause without beginning and a fruit without end. Since the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is beyond all dependence, it cannot be negated; therefore, it is said to be named the "Crossing of the True Mark."

Regarding the statement, "Because the Teacher of the Buddhas has been delivered, all Buddhas are also delivered": since the objective realm (*viṣaya*) is already free from dependence, wisdom (*jñāna*) is likewise free from dependence, for there is no duality between the realm and wisdom.
Although this clarifies wisdom, its primary purpose is to demonstrate the objective realm.
The passage beginning with "The Treatise says" is a verse from the *Vyākhyā* (Śāstra) praising Prajñā.
Because the object gives rise to wisdom, it is called the Buddha’s "Welcome";
because wisdom illuminates the object, it is called the Buddha’s "Reaching the Bottom."
