Each [master] has attained one particular path; therefore, it is said that this meaning is not non-existent.
Now, as for using principle to explain the *satyas*, this is precisely the interpretation of Xinghuang.

Thus, the sub-commentary below states: "Xinghuang says that what is called a *satya* is simply Buddha-nature and *nirvāṇa*. It is neither object nor wisdom, neither outflow (*āsrava*) nor non-outflow, neither cause nor fruit, and neither mundane nor supramundane; therefore, it is named the Noble Truth (*āryasatya*)."
This is an explanation based on principle.

However, since there are now four distinct types of the Four Noble Truths according to a single principle as they correspond to various capacities, the explanation provided by Xinghuang is not entirely satisfactory.
It is logical that the object (*viṣaya*) is correct because the object is a phenomenon (*dharma*), and phenomena fundamentally rely upon principle (*li*); therefore, the object is correct.
It is also logical that both wisdom (*jñāna*) and teaching (*śāsana*) are correct because wisdom arises in reliance upon the object, and the teaching is expounded in reliance upon wisdom.

Regarding the phrase "by means of principle" (*yili*) below: Principle is the foundation of object, wisdom, and teaching; since citing the foundation encompasses the branches, it is only by explaining the meaning of the truths (*satya*) through principle that the interpretation is fully consistent.
"That which can give rise to what is given rise to" refers to the habitual cause (*vāsanā-hetu*) that invites the fruit of suffering (*duḥkha-phala*).

"That which is produced further produces that which can produce" means that upon the fruit of suffering, one again gives rise to the cause of origination (*samudaya*); since the cause further invites the fruit, it is called the "revolving of suffering and origination.
"The Path is named 'that which can destroy'" means that precept, concentration, and wisdom are able to remedy suffering and origination.
"Extinction is that which is destroyed" means that the cessation of suffering and its origin is called the Truth of Extinction (*nirodha-satya*).
Regarding "mutual arising and extinction": when the agent of destruction arises, that which is destroyed ceases—this refers to the Noble Ones (*ārya*);
when that which is destroyed arises, the agent of destruction ceases—this refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding "affliction" (*pīḍā*) and so forth, these correspond respectively to the Four Noble Truths.

As for the phrase "as in the Sūtra," this refers to the three passages explained below within the wisdom regarding the Four Noble Truths in the "Chapter on the Four Truths" (*Catuhsatyaparivarta*) and the "Chapter on Noble Practices" (*Āryacaryāparivarta*); the concluding phrase "as in the Sūtra" in each case points to both chapters.
"Having immeasurable marks" means that the Four Truths are elucidated by way of the ten realms.
"Understanding suffering as being without suffering" means that the aggregates and sense bases are all suchness, so there is no suffering to be abandoned;
afflictions are themselves bodhi, so there is no origin of suffering to be severed.
Extremes and deviations are all the Mean and Right; there is no Path to be cultivated.
Birth-and-death is itself Nirvana; there is no extinction to be realized.
Therefore it is said that even the understanding of extinction as non-extinction is entirely the One Mind and the Three Truths; thus it is said that "therein exists the Real."
The cause of suffering is *samudaya* (origination); the cessation of suffering is *nirodha* (cessation); the remedy for suffering is *mārga* (the path).
Regarding "the one contains the immeasurable and so forth": the "one" refers to the single, ultimate Four Noble Truths, while the "immeasurable" refers to the three types of Four Noble Truths.

Regarding the taking of that which is countered by the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) to serve as its function: it is within the spheres of suffering (*duḥkha*), origination (*samudaya*), and cessation (*nirodha*) that the meaning of "function" becomes manifest.
Below the term "Tamer" (*vināyaka*), Kāśyapa asks:
"How is it that the various Tamers joyfully proclaim the True Reality (*satya*)?"
Therefore, the Buddha answered him with the single chapter on the "Four Truths.
That it is simply one without differentiation is precisely where the profound subtlety lies in the previous explanation of the truths (*satya*) from the perspective of principle (*li*).

Regarding the missing chapter herein: this is not part of the original text, but rather a passage concerning the meaning of "non-arising" that was omitted from an ancient manuscript. Later scholars collated it and marked it with a slip on the scroll or noted it outside the main text; however, some scribes, failing to understand this, inadvertently inserted it into the body of the text.

Furthermore, beneath the word "thus" (evam) in the commentary, there are two characters written in white ink marking it as a point of emphasis; these were also originally intended to be written twice within the main text, but they were omitted from the commentary manuscript and subsequently marked by the collator.
Now, the emphasis was placed beneath the character "rú" (如是), yet the scribe, not understanding this, also wrote it into the body of the text.
This saying is proven by the parrot’s mimicry.

Now, regarding this meaning of the non-arising of non-arising, if one wishes to explain it by way of analogy, it is as clarified in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* through the four propositions: namely, arising from arising, arising from non-arising, non-arising from arising, and non-arising from non-arising.

Arising from arising is the ignorance of birth-and-death; arising from non-arising is the liberation of the virtue of severance; non-arising from arising is the Prajñā of the virtue of wisdom; and non-arising from non-arising is the Dharma-body as the essence of principle.

These four phrases are both one and four, and both four and one. To facilitate easy understanding, they are presented as follows: the total recitation of the four phrases constitutes the Name; "non-arising non-arising" constitutes the Essence; "non-arising arising" constitutes the Thesis; "arising non-arising" constitutes the Function; and such an exposition constitutes the Teaching. Thus, not only is the meaning of the Sūtra’s essence clarified, but its other meanings are also revealed.
Regarding the five kinds of nature: the primary cause (正因) pertains to principle (理), while the remaining four pertain to phenomena (事).
Because it pertains to principle, although it is neither cause nor effect, its essence pervades both cause and effect.
The objective realm that serves as the causal condition for the arising of wisdom is already a cause;
furthermore, in relation to the fruit, wisdom itself is also a cause.
Therefore, it is called the "cause of causes."

Regarding the nature of the "fruit of fruits": since the merit of bodhi-wisdom is already a fruit, one further attains the fruit of the merit of nirvāṇa-cessation; thus it is called the "fruit of fruits.

The section beginning with "Now, for the time being" provides a direct demonstration by way of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), because the objects of the five aggregates are constantly present before one.

Therefore, in the initial stages of śamatha and vipaśyanā, one contemplates only the aggregates (skandhas); the nine [categories] such as the afflictions (kleśas) and so forth are contemplated only when they arise.
Now, following the essential point, the five natures (pañca-gotra) are demonstrated by means of the objective sphere of the aggregates.
Regarding "the reason why [the five aggregates] are below": "so-yi" (所以) refers to the underlying principle or meaning.

The five aggregates are phenomena (*dharma*), while the Buddha-nature is the principle (*li*); phenomena evolve from the principle, and these very phenomena are identical to that principle; therefore, it is called "the reason why."
The five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are causes; furthermore, they give rise to the cause of wisdom, and are therefore called "the cause of causes" (hetu-hetu).
Question:
The five aggregates are effects; why are they termed "causes"?
Answer: The delusive fruits of ordinary beings are still causes when compared to the Buddha.
As for "increasing and perfecting wisdom," both partial realization and ultimate attainment are termed increasing and perfecting wisdom.
That which is to be extinguished is precisely ignorance; the place where ignorance is extinguished is the fruit of nirvana.
"All other dharmas" refers to the elements (dhātus), the sense bases (āyatanas), and so forth.
Regarding "the nature of the fruit and the fruit" as the name: this is because the sutra is titled *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Regarding "the correct nature" as the essence: this is because the correct nature is the wondrous principle.
Regarding "the nature of the cause of causes and the nature of the fruit" as the thesis: this is because cause and effect constitute the thesis.
Question:
Since you take cause and effect as your primary tenet, why do you not include *nirvāṇa* as the fruit of cessation? Answer:

In fact, it encompasses both; however, since the title of the scripture is established primarily according to the fruit-of-fruits (phala-phala) and this is thus more convenient, it is appropriate that it be so named.
If one follows the previous principle, it should also be said that the name is established by "comprehensively subsuming the five natures" (*pañca-gotra*).

Regarding "the causal nature functions as the activity": since the twelve links of dependent origination are that which is to be negated, the meaning of the "capable" [nature] being revealed is thereby clarified.

As for "duality is non-duality," "duality" refers to cause and effect, while "non-duality" is the essence of principle; because phenomena and principle are fused into one, they are mutually identical and non-dual.

Regarding "it cannot be made into two": if one differentiates by means of names and phenomena, then the non-dual essence cannot serve as the fundamental principle of cause and effect; therefore, it is said that it cannot be made into two. The subsequent phrase is explained by analogy.
Below the phrase "having already established," the five chapters are formally set forth by distinguishing between names and phenomena (*nāma* and *vastu*).
"The vital point of practice" refers to what is essential, like the throat of a body or the collar of a garment.
There is nothing that surpasses cause and effect, for causes encompass all manner of goodness and effects subsume all manner of virtue.
Briefly stated, there are three types: namely, the three cultivations, the five practices, and the single practice.
Since these are explained in sequential order, they are not listed at the outset.
Question:

The *Weimo jing xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) states: "Nirvāṇa is not without the causes of the five practices; however, while the primary cause is the fruit, the secondary causes are the conditions, and thus the fruit is taken as the central tenet."
Furthermore, the preceding sentence states, "Do not overstep cause and effect. Why, then, are only three passages clarifying the cause cited to explain the meaning of the central thesis?
Answer: Although passages concerning the cause are cited, since the cause necessarily brings about its fruit, this is identical in meaning to the preceding sentence.
The brief indications in the *Fujing* (Scripture of the Talisman) are identical in meaning to the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Vimalakīrti).
Below, it is called the "threefold cultivation," which can attain the fruit of permanence and constitute the food of nirvāṇa.
Among the five practices, it is said that after cultivating these practices, one attains twenty-five samādhis and dwells in great nirvāṇa.
In the "Chapter on King of Virtue," this refers to reaching the other shore; in the "Chapter on the Lion’s Roar," it refers to dwelling in great nirvāṇa.
Within a single line, there is the Mahāyāna Great Nirvāṇa.

All such [terms] are the fruits to be realized; thus we know that the intent of clarifying the causes lies in the fruits. This is precisely the intent of clarifying the central theme (*mūla*) of this sutra, because this sutra correctly discusses the fruit—the realization attained by those who have perfected it.
"Rejecting the bhikṣus" means rejecting the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) by means of the Perfect [Vehicle].
"Manifesting that which is neither eternal nor impermanent" refers to the essence manifested through cause and effect.
The "inferior threefold cultivation" refers to the impermanence that is to be negated.

Regarding the phrase "this is the fuel for afflictions," it is because those of the Two Vehicles still possess ignorance in its entirety; thus, the "superior threefold cultivation" corresponds to abiding in cause and effect.
The food of nirvāṇa refers to the principle that is realized; both the partial principle and the ultimate principle are termed "food.
The four assemblies refer to the forty true causes.
This refers to those who relish [the Dharma]: because wisdom can realize the principle, it is likened to relishing sweetness.
"To tread and practice" means to step upon the essence of one's nature and cultivate the causes until the fruit is attained.
Regarding "the Dharma is constant," etc.: "Dharma" refers to the objective realm traversed, while "Buddha" refers to the wisdom that traverses it.
As for the meaning of "increasing or decreasing": increasing refers to adding up to two or three, while decreasing refers to reducing down to two or one.

Regarding "setting aside matters to focus on principles": the bhikṣus set aside the practical practices of the Hīnayāna and instead praised before the Buddha the principle-observations of the three contemplations—suffering, impermanence, and non-self—from the former teachings.
Therefore, a sutra says: "Just as among all footprints the elephant's footprint is foremost, so too is this perception of impermanence.
To cite a superior principle to refute an inferior one: suffering and the like are inferior principles, while permanence, bliss, self, and purity are superior principles.
Question:
Why are there only three types of cultivation mentioned? Answer:
The confusion regarding the fruit and the realization has been addressed; since the present discussion clarifies the meaning of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it is not mentioned here.
Since increase and decrease depend upon the capacities of practitioners (*yogin*), they should likewise extend up to the fourth [fruit].
The section beginning with "The second" explains the causes of cultivation by way of the five successive practices.
Regarding "the first refers to precepts, concentration, and wisdom": because among the five practices, the noble practice (ārya-caryā) occupies the first position, it is called "the first.
Since the noble practice does not exceed three types, precepts, concentration, and wisdom are specified.
Below the section on "Living at Home," the text is explained in successive order.
The initial passage concerns the holy practice of the precepts, as the sutra states: "Living at home is not joyful, being like a prison; leaving home is open and vast, being like empty space."

Regarding the phrase "brahmacarya" (pure conduct) mentioned in the text, it does not refer to the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*), but rather indicates that leaving the household life constitutes brahmacarya, because one thereby departs from the defilements of the household life.
This clarifies the noble practice of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Below the section "From the Head," it clarifies the noble practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is specifically the *vītarāga-dhyāna* (the dhyāna of transcendence).
Although the cited text is brief, it involves both cultivation and realization; "from head to foot" refers to the process of cultivation.
"Only this" and below constitutes the realization.
This realization of such extraordinary excellence involves opening the granary of the body to fully perceive the thirty-six constituents of one's own person.
"Contemplating" and below clarifies the noble practice of wisdom.

There are four modes of wisdom-practice: first, contemplating the eight sufferings and so forth as arising and ceasing; next, non-arising; next, the immeasurable; and finally, the unconditioned. These are evident in the text.
"As stated in the sutra" refers to the eleventh fascicle.
"Attaining twenty-five samādhis" refers to the fruit of the practice of wisdom (*prajñācaryā*), which is accomplished through that practice.
Specifically, it means attaining twenty-five samādhis upon the stage of fearlessness (*abhaya-bhūmi*) in order to benefit sentient beings according to their capacities.
The phrase "partial realization of the three virtues is called abiding in nirvāṇa, let alone emerging from it" uses the partial fruit to illustrate the emergence from the ultimate fruit.
"From shallow to deep" means that the cause is shallow while the fruit is deep.
From "Manifesting the Non-" below, the principle of the double negation is revealed through the facts of cause and effect.

From "Virtue King" below, five lines clarify the realization by means of cultivating the ten virtues; thus, that chapter states: "The Bodhisattva practices the Mahāparinirvāṇa and realizes the ten merits."

However, while the five elements are universally verified and the ten virtues are universally cultivated, one sets aside the secondary to adopt the primary in order to distinguish between the two, as discussed in detail in the *Sūji*.
Regarding the four elements being like a chest: the elements are like venomous snakes and the body is like a chest; the four elements forming the body is like snakes within a chest.
The five aggregates are like assailants; this refers to the sutra’s statement that "five caṇḍālas follow him with drawn swords," the full text of which is extensive.

As for "cutting off the currents," the currents are a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*) and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); from the perspective of their cause, they are called the river of afflictions, and from the perspective of their result, they are called the river of birth-and-death.
In the sutras, there are generally six rivers, namely: afflictions (*kleśa*), birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), the pursuit of the wholesome, evil karma, Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), and nirvana.
From the section beginning with "The first [river] from... onwards, the twenty-fifth sutra contains ten sections:

first, fewness of desires; second, contentment; third, tranquility; fourth, diligence; fifth, right mindfulness; sixth, right concentration; seventh, right wisdom; eighth, liberation; ninth, praise of liberation; and tenth, transforming sentient beings through nirvana.
Now, the first, second, and tenth [stages] are cited, while those in between are all omitted; hence the phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*).
The passage beginning with "Furthermore, good" is found in the twenty-ninth [chapter].

He said: "If one perceives the precepts, the characteristics of the precepts, the causes of the precepts, the fruits of the precepts, the superior aspects of the precepts, the inferior aspects of the precepts, the accumulation of the precepts, the oneness of the precepts, the duality of the precepts, these precepts, those precepts, the cessation of the precepts, the equality of the precepts, the cultivation of the precepts, the cultivator, or the perfection of the precepts—if there is such a perception, it is called not cultivating the precepts."
The commentary states:

To perceive the essence of the precepts as that which prevents the manifestations of transgression is what is called the "cause" during the stage of cultivation and the "fruit" at the time of accomplishment. From the noble above to the ordinary below, the multitude of precepts is termed a "collection. Whether taken collectively as one or individually as two, whether from oneself to others or from here to there, the cessation of faults is termed "extinction," while other virtues are termed "equality."
Cultivating the seven aforementioned gates is called the cultivation of precepts (*śīla-bhāvanā*).
One who cultivates these is said to have "precepts as their person," for the precepts can reach the fruit; thus they are called *pāramitās*.
To perceive such characteristics is called not cultivating the precepts.
The current text directly reveals the characteristics of cultivation; therefore, it says "not seeing" and so forth.

The same applies to concentration and wisdom: that is to say, concentration, the characteristics of concentration, the causes and fruits of concentration, and so on, are to be explained by analogy with the [preceding] explanation of precepts.
"To examine the beginning and trace the end" means that the beginning is the cause and the end is the fruit.

"There is nothing it does not move and nothing it cannot overcome" means that great causes and great fruits encompass everything; thus, the cause mobilizes myriad virtues and the fruit overcomes myriad merits. When cause and fruit are harmoniously integrated, principle is realized within phenomena.

Below "all," the perfect cause and perfect fruit universally integrate all things, which is termed being a person of non-obstruction; the lack of difference between the living and the Buddha is termed the One Path. Cultivating and realizing in this manner enables one to transcend the two deaths.
Regarding the practice of the ten perceptions (daśasaṃjñā) up to the knowledge of desire, these are all found in the thirty-fourth fascicle.
The Sūtra states: "If the fourfold assembly can cultivate the ten perceptions, one should know that such persons are able to attain nirvāṇa."
"First is the perception of impermanence, up to tenth is the perception of non-attachment.

Regarding "knowing the faculties and knowing the desires," the Sūtra says: "When a Bodhisattva, regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, knows the faculties and knows the causes; knows their inclusion and knows their increase; knows the master and knows the guide; knows the superior and knows the real; and knows the ultimate—then they may be called one who practices the pure holy life."
It is further stated: "The root of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment is the cause of desire; they are termed 'contact with clarity' (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*) and so forth.
Therefore, it is now said that the faculty of knowledge knows desire.

Regarding "connecting the Small and connecting the Shared": "Small" refers to the Tripiṭaka [Hīnayāna], by which the Perfect and Eternal Dharma draws in those of the two teachings and the three vehicles.
This refers to the general method of guidance, and thus it is said that "the Small [Vehicle] is received.

If one clarifies the three types of reception, however, this does not apply to Bodhisattvas of the Six Perfections nor to those of the Two Vehicles of the two teachings; a detailed explanation is provided in the *Sūtra Commentary* (*Shuji*).
Regarding "entering the sudden from the gradual," this is because the stages prior to the bhūmis are considered gradual, while ascending to the bhūmis is considered sudden.
The passage beginning with "The text says" cites the *Kāśyapa-parivarta* to substantiate this distinct meaning.
Regarding the phrase "When the foundation is established, the Way arises": when the foundation of *nirvāṇa* is established, then the various practices of the Way arise.
Is *nirvāṇa* not indeed the very foundation of practice?
The passage beginning with "Just as if there were no" means that if there were no main ropes, the subsidiary cords would not be aligned.
The hide represents *nirvāṇa*, while the hair and eyes represent the various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). "Mi" means "none.

Regarding the point that "the essential lies in the eternal": although the three modes of practice—partial, sequential, and perfect—differ, there is no distinction in their eternal fruit; therefore, the preceding text states, "Though the three differ, all take the eternal as their fundamental principle."
Regarding the phrase "practice meeting with the permanent": practice is the cause, and the permanent is the fruit.
The section beginning with "is able to manifest" refers to the principle manifested upon the fruit.

This is precisely the fundamental meaning of the preceding thesis; thus one knows that the thesis-fundamental (zongben) pertains to principle, the thesis-essence (zongyao) pertains to wisdom, and the thesis-aids (zongzhu) pertain to practice. By investigating the text through these categories, there will be no meaning that remains unclarified.
The "Seven Luminaries" refer to the sun, the moon, and the five planets.
Regarding the Northern Dipper (Beichen), the *Jingzhou Xingzhan* states: "The Northern Dipper is also named Tianguan and also named Beiji."
"The North Pole is the Purple Palace, the seat of Heaven.
As the *Analects* states: "To govern by means of virtue is like the North Star remaining in its place while the myriad stars revolve around it."
Regarding "resembling ten thousand," the *Book of Documents* states: "The Yangtze and Han rivers flow toward the sea as their lord.
Here, the seven luminaries and the myriad streams are metaphors for practice (*xing*), while the North Star and the Eastern Sea are metaphors for wisdom (*zhi*).

Regarding the phrase "or a person" (*kaścit puruṣaḥ*) and below: the person, principle, teaching, and practice are all able to provide assistance, causing the true partial realization (*bhāgavata-satya*) and the ultimate fruit (*phala*)—the eternal wisdom—to be manifested.

That is to say, by relying on the person one hears the teaching; by relying on the teaching one practices; and through practice one accords with the principle. By means of these four factors, one attains entry into the stage of partial truth and even the ultimate fruit; therefore, it is said that "one obtains power through assistance."

Regarding "the Path as an aid," the Path is principle; it also refers to using partial people and partial teachings as aids, as explained in the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) within the section on "Aids for Counteracting and Opening."
The passage beginning with "Like something worn-out" is a metaphor from the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*.
That sūtra states: "Suppose, for example, someone carrying a golden image travels to another country; having wrapped it in filthy and tattered rags, he abandons it in the wilderness."
Those who see them with the divine eye immediately inform the multitude.
When defilements are removed and the true form is revealed, all rejoice greatly.
My divine eye is likewise; observing those classes of sentient beings, entangled by evil karma and afflictions, fully beset by the sufferings of birth and death.
"Furthermore, one sees that within those sentient beings amidst the dust and defilements of ignorance, the Tathāgata-nature remains unmoving and cannot be destroyed.
The passage beginning with "the strong man" below is now the analogy in this sutra.
The "forehead jewel" is as previously cited.

Regarding the "Treasury of Jewels Sūtra," the "Tathāgatagarbha Chapter" states: "All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; from the very beginning, it has been constantly shrouded by immeasurable afflictions, and for this reason, sentient beings are unable to perceive it."
"It is like a poor woman’s house that contains a vast treasury of pure gold, yet none of her family members, young or old, know of its existence.
Regarding the phrase "in a well," the Sūtra says: "It is like a well and various kinds of treasures within a dark room; people know they are there, but because it is dark, they do not see them."
There is a skillful means that kindles a great bright lamp; by illuminating it, one is able to see.
This person never gives rise to the thought:
"This water and these jewels did not exist before, but now exist."
Nirvāṇa is likewise; it has existed from the very beginning and is not something that has only now come into being.
The Tathāgata of Great Wisdom, through skillful means, kindles the lamp of wisdom, enabling all bodhisattvas to perceive the Buddha-nature, which is the true cause of nirvāṇa.
"Those who are attached to these sentient beings do so because the mental continuum is not severed.
Regarding the phrase "merely in terms of," it means that while the principle is fundamentally one, there are differences according to time; therefore, it is said that the two times are different.
The character "ruò" (if) used here is an error.
Following the phrase "originally exists," although at the time of the spirit there is no actual occurrence of the future fruit, there nonetheless exists the principle of the future fruit.
The reading "time" (時) is an error for "assistance" (助).
"Golden mind" refers to Equal Enlightenment (等覺), and "seed-enlightenment" refers to Sublime Enlightenment (妙覺).
In the passage following "bright milk," milk is a metaphor for sentient beings, curd for Buddha-nature, and the warmth of the fermenting liquor for spiritual practice.
"Lao" (醪) should be read as "lao" (撈), meaning that when taking curdled milk (*dadhi*), one must certainly stir and scoop it.
Master Ying said: "It should be read as 'jiao' (酵), with the second character pronounced as 'xiao' (孝) in the ancient system; it refers to the yeast used for fermenting grain to produce wine."
In many instances, the scriptural text uses the character *láo* (pronounced as in "láo"),
which according to both the *Sāncāng* and the *Shuowén* refers to wine with dregs.
The character *láo* is not the correct orthography.
The sesame seeds are a metaphor for sentient beings; the oil is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature; and the pounding and pressing are metaphors for spiritual practice.

Regarding the inclusion of these two passages: the passage on the "Tathāgata-nature" is taken to prove that [the Buddha-nature] is inherently present, while the passages from the "Lion's Roar" and "Kāśyapa" chapters are taken to prove that it will be realized in the future.
The phrase "Furthermore, it quotes" refers to the *Kāśyapa-parivarta*, which states: "That which is not Buddha-nature is taught as being Buddha-nature.
That which is not Buddha-nature refers to such things as walls, fences, tiles, and stones.
This master merely succeeds in excluding references to wood and stone; how could he understand the principle that the environment and its inhabitants are mutually interfused?
One should know that the lands, atoms, and dust motes are all transformations of the mind, and that their very substance is the mind itself.
When my mind attains Buddhahood, all things within the dust motes of a world-system attain it simultaneously; how could wood and stone exist separately outside of the mind?
Thus, that which is not the originally inherent function refers to the fact that sentient beings possess this originally inherent function, whereas wood and stone do not.

Would you rather understand the principle of the mutual fusion of the environment and the inhabitants within the cause, or the fact of the mutual fusion of the environment and the inhabitants within the fruit?
As for the fault of "the fruit existing within the cause," this refutes their interpretation; such a fault is identical to that of the non-Buddhist outsiders.
If the continuum were permanent, it would reach the fruit by means of the continuity of causes;
yet it would also follow that it reaches the impermanent. This objection likewise arises because others do not understand the meaning of the two birds flying together.
If one realizes the dual movement, then both the permanent and the impermanent are inherently complete within the principle.

Regarding the statement that "the revealing cause reveals what is originally present" and so forth: the revealing cause is wisdom, which illuminates the nature that is originally present, just as a lamp illuminates objects.
The cause of birth is merit; from cause to fruit, it is like clay forming a jar.
Regarding the "Crab and Oyster" passage below, the Master now refutes both schools simultaneously.
As for those who hold dogmatic views, he does not permit them to be exclusively refuted.
As for those who exclusively refute others, they do not permit exclusive adherence.
To engage in mutual claims of right and wrong is like the war between the wren and the clam, both of whom were simultaneously captured by the fisherman, our Master of the Present.
The tenth chapter of the *Chunqiu Houyu* states: "When the Marquis of Zhao was about to invade Yan, Su Dai spoke on behalf of Yan to the King of Zhao, saying:
'I have come from abroad and passed by a small stream where I saw an oyster basking in the sun.'"
The stork pecked at its flesh, while the clam clamped its beak.
The stork said,

Although they are used individually at times, the Buddha’s intention is necessarily to employ them in tandem; thus, one knows that using them singly does not forfeit their dual application.
Regarding "because of mastery in application," this means that either individually or together, it is appropriate.

In the section following "good and evil," by way of analogy, the inclusion of good and the inclusion of evil also constitute dual engagement; yet there is no contradiction in the distinction between single and dual application, which is why it says "either used simultaneously or sequentially."

Regarding the phrase "the heterodox are those such as the non-Buddhists," at the beginning of that chapter, the Tathāgata first addressed Ājñātakauṇḍinya, discussing the permanence of the five aggregates and establishing the practice of right contemplation; thus, one abandons impermanent form and attains permanent form, and so forth.
One who can know in this way is called a śramaṇa and a brāhmaṇa.
This was intended to refute the heterodox practitioners who falsely claim such titles while lacking any genuine practice.
Upon hearing this, the heterodox teachers became filled with resentment and subsequently requested a debate; there were ten heterodox teachers in total, the tenth of whom was Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.
Because this person employs skillful means, they are included within the correct gathering.

Thus the Sūtra says: "This Brahmin, in the distant past, at the time of the Buddha Samantaprabha, gave rise to the bodhicitta; long ago he thoroughly penetrated and fully understood the characteristics of dharmas, yet for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests as dwelling among the non-Buddhist paths."
Regarding "the 'evil' refers to the various māras and their like," this corresponds to the sutra which says: "The World-Honored One, having known this, addressed Cunda:
'Where is the bhikṣu Ānanda now?'"
He replied: "The bhikṣu Ānanda is outside the Śāla grove, twelve yojanas from this great assembly, where he is being harassed and disturbed by sixty-four trillion māras."

"Regarding 'equally encompassing all': this does not merely refer to encompassing Kauṇḍinya and Ānanda, but also encompasses the non-Buddhists and all Māras, bringing them together into the secret treasury.
To 'see this meaning' and so forth means to see the three intentions of the inconceivable dual movement and dual encompassment."
Possessing these three, it is called skillful mastery in application (*vaśitā-prayoga-kuśala*).

Regarding the four "followings" (*anuvartana*): the *Dhyāna-sūtra* calls them "followings," while the *Mahā-śāstra* calls them "completions. These refer to following one's inclination, following what is appropriate, following the remedy, and following the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Those who abide in Śūraṅgama refer to both provisional abiding and ultimate abiding; they are all able to give rise to the functions of the ten realms, and thus it is said that they manifest in various ways.
Although they manifest throughout the day, they do not depart from Śūraṅgama, and thus it is said that they do not move from the dharma-nature.
Regarding the passage "As for that vision," those who see the form and hear the voice both receive the four benefits.

If one considers the fundamental function (*mūla-vṛtti*) to be the essence (*tattva*), it is the essence because the fundamental function resides in principle (*li*); it is the thesis (*siddhānta*) because the functional application (*vṛtti*) pertains to the fruit (*phala*); and it is the function (*vṛtti*) because it freely transforms others.
Regarding the phrase "from the hands emerge fragrant-colored milk and so forth," this refers to the text of the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*.

Interpreting it now through contemplative understanding, the two hands symbolize the two wisdoms; the emergence of milk symbolizes the preaching of the Dharma, thereby causing others to be satiated with the flavor of the teachings.
"The old physician who steals the teaching" refers to non-Buddhists stealing the Buddha's teachings.
Because they employ the names of the Buddha’s permanence and bliss, it is said that "they pilfer the name of milk.
Regarding the phrase "does not understand," it means they do not understand the true meaning of the four virtues.

Regarding the phrase "and thus," because one does not understand the four virtues, the four inversions arise: one falsely conceives of the continuous succession of moments as permanent; one falsely conceives of the pleasant experiences of humans and devas as blissful; one falsely conceives of shifting autonomy as a self; and one falsely conceives of this foul body covered by thin skin as pure. Deceived by these four matters, one gives rise to the four inversions.

Below the phrase "poisonous confusion," it means that the poison of the four inversions (catur-viparyāsa) stifles and disturbs the true mind, thereby wounding the Dharma-body (dharma-kāya) and harming the life-force of wisdom.
The metaphors of salt, bitterness, and sourness represent the three types of cultivation.
"Using a wedge to extract a wedge" (yǐ qiè chū qiè) is also written as "qiè" (pronounced with the initial *q* and the final *-ie*, first tone).
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Qiè means a wedge (*xiān*).
Xiān is pronounced with the initial *z* and the final *-lin*."
By means of the wedge of correct milk, one extracts the wedge of false milk.
Alternatively, those who explain the Dharma of skillful means use the impermanence of the Lesser Vehicle to counteract false permanence.
Alternatively, it is said that the "True Dharma" uses the perfect and eternal to remedy the impermanent.
This refers to the ten practices of the Separate Teaching (biejiao), which benefit others according to their capacities.
As for the phrase "as in the sutra," this refers to the text of the "Chapter on Lamentation" (Aitan pin).
The calf is a metaphor for the Buddha.

Attaining the Middle Way, being gentle, harmonious, and compliant is called "well-tamed"; it neither gallops toward emptiness nor dwells in existence, neither abiding on the high plateau of nirvana nor residing in the low-lying marshes of saṃsāra.
The samādhi of the untainted ultimate truth is like not drinking wine;
the samādhi of non-attachment to conventional truth is like not eating dregs.
The wisdom of nirvāṇa is easy to attain, like walking upon smooth grass.
Discriminative wisdom is difficult to produce, like the husks of wheat;
it is like a barren cow having no milk, which serves as a metaphor for the absence of compassion, thereby clarifying that the Buddha possesses unique (āveṇika) compassion.

Regarding the transformation of the ordinary person into a sage, this refers to the Distinct Teaching (bhedavyavahāra), wherein the ordinary being prior to the stages is transformed into a sage who has attained the stages (bhūmi).
"Also 'transforming'" (亦革) refers below to transforming the ten stages of the sages to achieve the unsurpassed path of wondrous enlightenment.

"'Buddha-teaching'" (佛教) refers below to the non-duality of the beginning and end in perfect faith and perfect cultivation; therefore, it says "immediately attains abiding in [the stage of]... and so forth.
Regarding the meaning of the "four exits" (*catur-niḥsaraṇa*), it refers to the verse on "that which was originally non-existent now existing.
The Master of Men named this the "Four Exits Verse" (*catur-niḥsaraṇa-gāthā*) and also called it the "Four Pillars Verse" (*catur-stambha-gāthā*).
Thus, *nirvāṇa* is like a room, and the four exits are like its pillars.
First, it appears in the "Bodhisattva Chapter"; second, it appears in the "Brahmacarya Chapter"; third, it appears in the twenty-fifth fascicle; and fourth, it appears in the twenty-sixth fascicle.
The general meaning is the same, yet they differ in terms of their function as conditions.

First, it explains the difference and non-difference of a single bodhisattva; second, it explains attainment and non-attainment; third, it explains that existence is not necessarily existent and non-existence is not necessarily non-existent; fourth, it explains the absence of fixed nature in order to refute fixed natures. Therefore, it is said that it clarifies "non-differentiation and differentiation," and so forth.
To take this as an example of what is faultless: it parallels those four departures, explaining that milk has many varieties.
When "false milk" is called "milk-milk," birth and death are metaphorically likened to milk, while nirvana is likened to non-milk.
"Since the cause and effect of an ordinary person arise together, it is called 'milk-milk.
Why must you, my son, be confused? This concludes the reproach directed at the questioner. "Son" is a term of honor for a man.

Regarding those who go to a teacher to study writing: in this region, in ancient times, when a child was six years old, they were taught arithmetic and the names of directions; at ten, they entered the primary school (*xiǎoxué*) to study the *liùjiǎ* (the sixty-day cycle), writing, and accounting—this is what is meant by "literature" (*wénxué*).
The "Discourse on Emerging from Desire" clarifies that the Brahmā Heaven transcends the desire realm.
The "Heaven of Śakra" refers to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Regarding works such as the *Cang-ya*, there are many varieties; for instance, the *Cang* includes the *Cangjie pian*, the *Beicang*, and the *Sancang*.
The *Yǎ* (Elegant) school includes the *Guǎngyǎ*, the *Bóyǎ*, and the *Xiǎoyǎ*.
"Cāng" (Cang) is a personal name.
The *Dìwáng Shìjì* states: "Huangdi hung his robes; Cangjie created writing."
"E" (Er) is not a personal name;
it means "near. Because its breadth of learning and knowledge can be approached for the purpose of attaining correctness, it is called the *Erya*.
Mr. Xie correctly cites the *Cangjie* to prove that *Brahma* and *Kharoṣṭhī* are names of persons; the *Yaliang* follows suit.

As for the phrase "two worldly [terms]," it is analogous to how the two books of this land, the *Cangjie* and the *Yaliang*, both describe the glosses and definitions of written characters and designate them as "two-character [names]."
Thus, Brahmā is one person and Kharoṣṭhī is another person.
"Bawa" is the sound of a child's first attempts at speech; it is used as a metaphor for the minor teachings of skillful means.

Regarding what are called the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are conditioned; the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*) are unconditioned. These are termed the two truths of arising and ceasing, and thus constitute the two characters.

Regarding the "half" and "full" as two characters: the aforementioned conditioned and unconditioned combined constitute the "half-character," which is contrasted with the "great" [teaching] to be called "full."
Regarding "the six practices are all manifest," this refers to the cultivation of three superior and three inferior [aspects] respectively.

As for the statement that "this is Mahāyāna, yet not complete," the intention is that if one were to speak of both superior and inferior aspects of *nirvāṇa*, then both the Great and Small Vehicles would be fulfilled, and thus it would be called "complete.
However, because the *Lotus Sūtra* abolishes the Small Vehicle, this [Mahāyāna] is not yet complete.
Regarding the phrase "by this, it is impermanent," the character "you" (由) should be read as "you" (猶), meaning that while discussing permanence, one refers to being in *nirvāṇa*.

From the words "this entire" (*cidiu*) below, the *Lotus Sūtra* reveals the provisional to manifest the real, transcending all other teachings; what has been, is now, and will be explained is the most supreme, yet it is here said not to be complete.
While the "eternal abiding of worldly phenomena" and "knowing that dharmas are eternally without self-nature" explicitly discuss permanence, it is here said to be impermanence.
Being non-sagely and contrary to the scriptures, his confusion was extreme; he could not be engaged in discussion, hence it is said that there is no need for debate.
The five points of Xinghuang are roughly as described in the *Sujì*.
To "criticize the small and praise the great" means to criticize the Tripiṭaka [Teaching] and praise the Three Teachings.
To "retain the partial" means to retain the Two Vehicles.
To "abolish the partial and clarify the full" means that, if explained according to the Four Teachings, then the latter three teachings all receive the name of "full."
If one refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, then the former three [teachings] are all "half-letters," while only the Perfect [Teaching] is called "complete.

To open the half and clarify the complete means that the provisional [teaching] is discarded in terms of relative dependence, while the opening [of the half] is established in terms of absolute non-dependence.
Thus we know that while the two terms "Half" and "Full" share a common name, their meanings differ.
Subhadra is translated here as "Well-Virtuous.
The "Chapter on Cunda" states: "Outside the Śāla grove there was a brahmin named Subhadra."
At the age of one hundred and twenty, he attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and conceived the notion that he had entered nirvana.
The Buddha ordered Ānanda to summon him and taught him the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), whereby he attained the fruit of arhatship.
As for those who hear of the Perfect and Eternal yet realize only the Lesser Fruit, it is because a small portion [of the Great] is itself the Great Fulfillment.
To clarify the two characters "Ever-Abiding" (changzhu) is as explained in the "Chapter on Lamentation."
The section beginning with "Furthermore, regarding the fetters" below summarizes them into four propositions based on five periods.

The first proposition refers to the Deer Park; the second, to the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; the third, to the two flavors (*dvi-rasa*); and the fourth, to the teachings prior to the Deer Park period.

Regarding "The three perversions," the first section explains them in terms of perverse wisdom (*mithyā-prajñā*), and the second explains them in terms of perverse meditative concentration (*mithyā-dhyāna*).
For example, grasping at a flash of lightning that quickly extinguishes serves as a metaphor for how false permanence does not endure.
The moth flying into a flame is a metaphor for how illusory pleasure is nothing but suffering.
The silkworm binding itself in its cocoon is a metaphor for how the illusory self is not autonomous.
The section beginning with "pursuit" clarifies that because one gives rise to false attachments, one pursues the five sensory objects (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
The section beginning with "Furthermore" explains this in terms of *vitarka-vicāra* (erroneous dhyāna).
This refers to the contemplation of the six aspects (*ṣaḍvidhākāra*).

In the branch of *vitarka-vicāra* within the first dhyāna, non-Buddhists cultivate a sense of weary detachment toward *vitarka* and *vicāra*, regarding the first dhyāna as suffering, coarse, and an obstruction.

Because these two factors disturb the concentrated mind, they are suffering; because joy and pleasure arise from these two factors, they are coarse; and because these two factors obscure higher concentrations, they are obstacles.
The second dhyāna is different from this; thus it is called "superior, sublime, and transcendent."
The cultivation of the three higher *dhyānas* and the four *ārūpya-samāpattis* is likewise.
This aversion to the lower three and aspiration for the upper three may also be termed "perverse cultivation of the three.
The passage beginning with "capable of destroying desire and defilement" clarifies that these three types of cultivation possess the power to destroy delusions.
“Defilement” (rañjana) refers to craving (*rāga*).
Regarding “wandering among the flowers of awakening” (*bodhi-puṣpa*): since the seven factors of awakening (*sapta-bodhyaṅga*) are like flowers, they are called “awakening-flowers.

In the passage beginning with “Furthermore, practicing erroneously,” the text of the *Śoka-parivarta* contains only the two types of *ī*—the new and the old. Now, based on the meaning, the worldly *ī* and the neither-new-nor-old *ī* are added; this follows the previous example of the single milk being analyzed into many varieties.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that for a Bodhisattva who relies on the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*), a name is established based on its meaning; thus it is called "Dharma-giving" (*dharma-dāna*).
This is an example of that principle.

However, while the sutra uses the old letter *i* as a metaphor for the outsiders, since the letter *i* of the world has now been established based on its meaning, the name of the old *i* is used to designate the Two Vehicles.

Regarding the existence of a separate commentary manuscript, it divides the "Profound Preface" preceding the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* into three sections—namely, the Fourfold *Siddhānta* in four fascicles, the Four Teachings in four fascicles, and the Three Contemplations in two fascicles; here, the reference is to the Four Teachings.

Regarding the statement "the treasuries of precepts, concentration, and wisdom": this means that the Vinaya Piṭaka elucidates the precepts, the Sūtra Piṭaka elucidates concentration, and the Abhidharma Piṭaka elucidates wisdom.
Because there are three distinct divisions of these treasuries, they are called the "Three Piṭakas"; this is an explanation of the meaning based on the compound term.
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, they are called "three" because they refer to the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
As for calling them "piṭakas" (baskets) on account of the sūtras, vinaya, and abhidharma, this is an analysis of the meaning based on the division of the characters.
Regarding "for those who are like infants," those of the three vehicles are all called infants; they progress through the cultivation of the three trainings as if ascending a flight of stairs.
Those who fear the long journey are unable to travel the five hundred *yojanas*.
The "resting at the conjured city" refers specifically to those of the Two Vehicles;
as for Bodhisattvas, they do not enter [the ultimate truth] during the causal stage, but enter it only upon reaching the fruit.

The section beginning with "Bodhisattva" below refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, who cultivate the three trainings of the Lesser Vehicle as auxiliary practices; these are also practitioners of gradual *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
The following clarifies that the same applies to both the general and specific [aspects].
The life-preserving bag is the minor precept; the white bones are the minor concentration; and the eight sufferings are the minor wisdom.

Regarding "penetrating both the near and the far": those of dull faculties penetrate the partial truth (pariniṣpanna-satya) nearby, while those of sharp faculties penetrate the Middle Way from afar—this refers to receiving and guiding people.
From the phrase "If one can" onwards, the text borrows from the *Lotus Sūtra*’s passage on the opening of the Lesser Vehicle to establish the meaning of the universal person’s reception and guidance.

Regarding the principles of the practices: as for the phenomena (*dharma*), they involve practicing through dust-motes of kalpas to enter emptiness and emerge into the provisional; as for the principle (*li*), it involves the initial mind knowing the Middle Way and its full development upon reaching the stages (*bhūmi*). Therefore, this is not something known by the three vehicles of the two teachings.

Since the ultimate truth realized by the bodhisattvas of both vehicles is identical to that of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), they are all subsumed within the category of the two vehicles.

Therefore, the previous statement that [this teaching] "is not shared with the two vehicles" serves to clarify that the aforementioned bodhisattvas do share it with the two vehicles; it is their domain.

Regarding the phrase "not known by the two vehicles of the lower stages": the teaching of the perfect fusion of the three truths is not something known by the two vehicles of the two-vehicle teaching, nor by those of the lower stages of the distinct teaching.
The "lower stages" refer to the stages prior to the [ten] grounds (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the realization of the Way being identical to the Perfect [Teaching], there is the aspect of knowledge.
As for progressing from shallow to deep, the three teachings each possess varying degrees of shallowness and depth, whereas the Perfect Teaching is exclusively profound.
Because the Bodhisattva fully cultivates the four teachings, it is said that they proceed from the shallow to the deep.

Regarding the phrase "namely, the gradual and sudden teachings," this refers to traversing the three partial and gradual teachings until reaching the perfect and sudden; therefore, it is called "gradual-sudden" and "gradual-perfect."

This refers to one type within the text: namely, the five successive stages from the gradual to the perfected, which correspond to the sequential *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* among the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

The phrase "Furthermore, there is" (復有) and the following line constitute the fifth section, which is not presented in sequential order; among the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, it refers specifically to the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Regarding the term "setting forth" (發軫), the *Wenxuan* states: "Setting forth at the mouth of the Qing Luo River," with the commentary noting: "Chen means 'a carriage.'"
The phrase "setting out from Luoyang" refers to the departure from the capital.
Here, the expression "setting forth the carriage" is used as a metaphor for the initial cultivation [of the path].

As for the statement that there is "no further distinction," it means that the Perfect Dharma (yuanfa) has no differentiation; because one enters it through the gradual [stages], it is called "gradual-perfection" (jianyuan).
It is not meant that the Perfect [Teaching] differs from the Gradual and Sudden;

rather, it is called "miscellaneous" because those for whom this teaching is intended—the practitioners of the Three Vehicles and those who are being grafted onto it—are not of a single type. Thus, it is termed "miscellaneous."

Regarding the sequential order of the teachings as illustrated by this analogy: the milk first produced from the cow represents the Buddha’s appearance in the world and his initial preaching of the *Avataṃsaka*; continuing until it finally transforms into ghee represents the Buddha’s final preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, as explained in the thirteenth fascicle.

"One should not grasp [the teachings] according to their relative depth" means that one should not claim that the *Milk* and other stages are definitively shallow and therefore inferior to the *Avataṃsaka*,
nor that the *Clarified Butter* is definitively deep and therefore superior to the *Nirvāṇa*.

One must understand that while there are five flavors based on their sequential arising, all these flavors are entirely interpenetrating and harmonious; therefore, there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority.

The teaching at the Deer Park reveals the absence [of such distinctions], yet they are also present in the secret [teachings]; this is not a matter of distinguishing superiority or inferiority based on whether a teaching has been opened or remains unopened.
The section beginning with "If one says" extensively cites various texts to refute fixed attachments.

Regarding the analogies for the shallow and deep views: if the four flavors were shallow, they should not be used as analogies for the deep; if the *amṛta* (clarified butter) were deep, it should not be used as an analogy for the shallow.

Regarding the physician’s diagnosis of the king’s illness and so forth: the physician is a metaphor for the Buddha; the king is a metaphor for sentient beings; the illness is a metaphor for clinging to impermanence; and the milk is a metaphor for this present sutra, which uses the medicine of permanence to cure the disease of impermanence.

Regarding the eight flavors of sweet ghee (*madhura-ghṛta*): when it is milk or curd, it is light; when it is clarified butter (*sarpis*), it is thick; and ghee occupies the middle stage, thus possessing all these flavors. These are: first, the flavor of raw milk; second, the flavor of cooked milk;

third, the flavor of ghee; fourth, the flavor of whey; fifth, the flavor of milk; sixth, the flavor of sweetness; seventh, the flavor of lightness; and eighth, the flavor of richness. These are used as metaphors for the eight virtues of *nirvāṇa*: permanence, bliss, selfhood, purity, eternal peace, stainlessness, coolness, and freedom from aging and death.
"Moreover, as for its profundity": "moreover" (況) is a term of comparison.
That which cannot be described as profound refers to the fact that the teachings of the Two Vehicles are shallow by comparison.
"As blood transforms into milk" means that ignorance is itself enlightenment, just as blood transforms into milk.
From the essence of the Dharma-realm to the dharmas of the realms refers to the teaching of the Perfectly Sudden (yuantun) based upon the principle of the Perfectly Sudden.
*The Profound Meaning of the Nirvana Sūtra: The Source and Essential Pivot*, Scroll Three;
*The Profound Meaning of the Nirvana Sūtra: The Source and Essential Pivot*, Scroll Four.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyuan of Qiantang, Song Dynasty.

Below the phrase “Like the Sun,” the sun is a metaphor for the essence of the *dharmadhātu*; its illumination is a metaphor for the phenomena of the *dharmadhātu*; and the high mountain is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva.

The passage beginning with "like the deaf" provides a metaphor for those of limited capacity who, while seated at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka*, fail to gain great benefit; being deaf, they cannot hear the Great [Teaching], and being mute, they cannot speak of the Great.
Regarding the phrase "concealing its... below: first, it concerns the concealment of the body; second, it concerns the concealment of the Dharma.
As for the initial passage: the body of Śrīdeha (Śubhavyūha) is concealed by the image of Śākyamuni sixteen feet tall.
The section beginning with "The manner of concealment" clarifies the hidden dharma.
The Tathāgatagarbha is the Perfect and Sudden Dharma; it enables ordinary beings to reform themselves and become Lesser Sages.
"Non-arising and non-functionality" means that rotten seeds do not sprout and damaged roots are useless.
"Giving first and taking away later" refers to giving the Small [Vehicle] at the Deer Park and taking it away with the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna).
Regarding "entrusting the business and taking charge of the wealth," this employs the parable of the poor son from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This parable illustrates entrusting the family business of the Mahāyāna in order to transform bodhisattvas.
The various Prajñāpāramitā sūtras are mostly dialogues between Śūnyatā-utpanna (Emptiness-born), Śāriputra, and Pūrṇa-maitrāyaṇīputra.
As for "entrusting the wealth and determining the nature," this refers to the assembly where the father and son establish their innate affinity.

As the sutra says, "This is truly my son, and I am truly his father," this serves as a metaphor for the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation of the provisional (*upāya*), wherein those of the two vehicles shall all become Buddhas.
The passage beginning with "The text says" refers to the ninth fascicle, specifically the eight thousand people mentioned in the "Dharani" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Thus we know that the events of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, such as the opening and gathering [of the assembly], are all designated as "ghee"; however, while those [texts] set aside this [current] bestowal, their meanings differ slightly.
However, because the fundamental intention of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has already been fully expressed, the teaching has now reached its final nirvana.
The section beginning with "Now, as for the multitude" generally demonstrates the underlying purpose of the transformation.
Sentient beings inherently possess [this nature], no different from that of the Buddhas; yet, unaware of it in their daily lives, they sink into the cycle of birth and death.

Therefore, the Buddha appeared in the world and, using the two types of wisdom as his fingers, pointed out the deluded followers and revealed their original nature. Just as he was about to manifest this directly, he feared they might slander the Dharma; since their capacities were not uniform, he established the five periods of teaching. By combining the distinct and the limited with the three vehicles and the two truths, he matured them over one lifetime before finally opening up the provisional teachings—this is why the *Lotus Sūtra* and the present scripture arose.
The section beginning with "Or, [the Buddha] composed" describes the five periods.
Because the *Avataṃsaka* belongs exclusively to the Separate and Perfect [Teachings], it is "Great";
because the Deer Park [teaching] consists only of the Tripitaka, it is "Small."
The Vaipulya sutras censure the partial and small while praising the perfect and great, intending to cause one to feel shame for the small and aspire to the great;
the Prajñāpāramitā entrusts the Great Dharma to them, causing the Bodhisattvas to gradually attain thorough understanding and ease;
the Lotus Sutra reveals the provisional means, establishing the fixed nature of the lineage.

The section beginning with "Sentient beings" clarifies that since they have already seen their Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they now [attain] *nirvāṇa* in this present sutra; thus, one should know that the meaning of seeing the nature in these two sutras is identical.

Regarding "tranquilly between the twin trees," this refers to what the Sūtra calls "lying on his right side," signifying that the period of his transformative activity has reached its culmination and that the merit of his internal wisdom in guiding others is now complete.
Regarding the "stilling of the two rivers" (*xi jiao er he*), this refers to what the sutra calls "tranquil and silent"; hence it is termed the "stilling of the teaching.
As for the two rivers: the larger is the Bahuda River to the south of the city, and the smaller is the Hiraṇyavatī River to the north of the city.
"A hundred *li* apart, the Buddha dwelt between them, attaining *nirvāṇa* beneath the trees of the four pairs and eight ranks.
Regarding the section beginning with "All Buddhas," Dīpaṃkara and Kāśyapa appeared in a pure land and, having preached only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, entered *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the phrase 'fragrant ointment applied to the three palaces,' some versions read 'six palaces. "Two palaces" refers to the palaces of the Emperor and the Crown Prince.

Zheng Xuan’s commentary states: "The 'six palaces' consist of one palace in front and five palaces behind.

"Later, when she was installed in the inner palace, her status became equal to that of the Son of Heaven.
As for the seven assemblies: first, bhikṣus; second, bhikṣuṇīs; third, śikṣamāṇās; fourth, śrāmaṇeras; fifth, śrāmaṇerikās; sixth, upāsakas; and seventh, upāsikās.
The six [categories], beginning with *bhikṣu*, have their names translated and meanings explained in full within the commentary (*śū*).
As for *śikṣamāṇā*, this is translated as "woman training in the Dharma"; she does not receive a separate set of precepts.

It is further stated:

Regarding the phrase "the radiance illuminates the seven assemblies," this means that once the fragrance of the precepts has been applied to the two palaces [of body and mind], the light of the Way shines far and wide upon the seven assemblies.

The *Ruiying tu* states: "Dew that is thick and sweet is called 'sweet dew' (*amṛta*).

“Amṛta (sweet dew) signifies benevolent grace; it is also called ‘Celestial Wine.
Regarding the phrase “as if waiting,” it means awaiting a wise person to expound this sutra, likening it to waiting for the Yellow River to become clear; this expresses how difficult such a thing is.

In the *Shiqian ji* by Prince Nian, it is said: "The Cinnabar Hills stand for a thousand years before being scorched once; the Yellow River remains clear for a thousand years before becoming turbid once. These are both regarded as great auspicious omens by the most sagacious sovereigns."
Furthermore, "When the Yellow River clears, a sage is born.
Zici of the *Zuo Zhuan* said: "There is a poem from the *Book of Zhou* that says:"
"To wait for the Yellow River to become clear—how long can human life last?

*Ju* means "how could it be" or "by no means."

"Having a fixed time but no specific day" means that although he had granted permission for the teaching and proclamation [of the scripture], because I have many obstacles, I ultimately had no day on which I could hear it.
"Dai" (逮) means "to reach" or "to arrive at.

Jinling is a place name; during the periods of the Wu, Jin, Song, Qi, Liang, and Chen dynasties, this region was called Jiangnan (South of the River), and all six dynasties established their capitals there.
The *Shilu of Jiankang* states: "Originally it was the district of Jinling in Chu; during the Qin dynasty it was changed to Moling; during the Wu dynasty it was changed to Jianye.
Because the name 'Ye' was the taboo name of Emperor Min of the Jin dynasty, it was changed to Jiankang."
Emperor Yuan ascended the throne and designated it the Jiankang Palace.

Regarding the "collapse like crumbling earth": in the eighth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Emperor Wen ordered Prince Jin Yang Guang and the Duke of Qinghe Yang Su to lead five hundred thousand troops to invade Chen. This statement regarding his "second emergence" from Jiangdu refers to the time when the author of the commentary was detained by illness in Hongzhou.

As for the phrase "Ding suffered from illness while in Yuzhang," "Ding" is the name by which the author of the commentary is known.

Since the Great Master had already departed from Jiangdu for a second time, while the Master of the Commentary remained ill in Hongzhou, he was unable to follow him.
"Since we are far removed from the Holy Master, how could we have heard this scripture?

This means that after his illness was cured at Yuzhang, he first raised his oars and unfurled his sails to travel swiftly to Jiangdu to visit the Wise One (Jizang).

However, he encountered Emperor Wen of the Sui on an eastern tour and Prince Jin entering the court; consequently, the Great Master turned eastward toward Mount Tai, and thus had no leisure to deliver lectures, instead remaining with me as I returned to the East.

Regarding "dongxuan" (returned): "xuan" may also be written as "huan" (to return), with a pronunciation similar to that of "quántóng" (泉同).

As for his departure from Jiangdu in spring and only arriving in autumn, this was because he traveled at a slow pace, seeking to benefit people wherever he went.

Regarding his entry into parinirvāṇa during winter: it was on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month of that year, at the hour of the Sheep (wei), that he passed away while sitting cross-legged before the statue of Maitreya at Shicheng Temple, west of Tiantai.
Regarding the phrase "Alas, for me, there are obstacles to the Dharma": *yi* (伊) means "indeed" (*wei*) and is merely a particle; *yu* (余) means "I.

First was the obstacle of encountering the Master's departure from the valley; second, the obstacle of the entanglements of formal visits and requests for instruction; third, the obstacle of the collapse of the Jinling earthworks; fourth, the obstacle of being subjected to further slaughter and plunder; fifth, the obstacle of still encountering mist and dew; sixth, the obstacle of lingering illness in Yuzhang; seventh, the obstacle of returning eastward to Mount Tai; eighth, the obstacle of encountering his entry into *parinirvāṇa* during winter.
Because eight matters obstruct me from hearing the Dharma, they are called "obstructions to the Dharma.
Had I not remained in the valley, I would have been able to hear it;
even though I am in the imperial court, if my affairs of petition and consultation were few, I would likewise have been able to hear it.
Although those people are closely interconnected, if Jinling were to remain in long-term peace, I would surely have had the opportunity to hear [the teachings].

Furthermore, even if he did not enter parinirvāṇa, despite the aforementioned obstacles, he would ultimately have delivered lectures so that I might have heard them; therefore, the obstacle to his entering parinirvāṇa was the most profound and grave.
Therefore, the following passage expresses this lament: "The sun has already set behind the layered cliffs, and the blind turtle sleeps at the bottom of the sea.

At that time, people were heard saying,
"The Tathāgata has appeared in the world.
Having heard this, the blind men returned and deliberated together, saying:
"If we were to encounter the Buddha, we would surely be saved," they thought,
and immediately asked others,
"In which country does the Buddha reside?"
He replied, "The Buddha is in Śrāvastī. Thereupon,
each of them begged for one gold coin to hire someone to lead the way.
At that time, there was a man who took the money and led the blind men to the kingdom of Magadha, where he abandoned them in a marshy wasteland.
Not knowing their location, the blind men grasped one another's hands and wandered across others' fields, damaging and destroying the seedlings and grain.
While the elder was tending his fields, he saw those [blind men] trampling the seedlings; he became exceedingly enraged.
The blind man sought his mercy and related the preceding events in detail; the elder then sent a messenger to take him to Śrāvastī.
Upon arriving in that country, he heard that the Buddha had gone to the kingdom of Magadha.
When he reached that country, he further heard that the World-Honored One had already returned to Śrāvastī.
Thus he pursued him, making a total of seven such journeys.
Knowing that his faculties were ripe, the Buddha waited for him in Śrāvastī.
When the blind man arrived at the Buddha’s presence, he was bathed in light and his vision was restored; the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the state of an Arhat.
Regarding the phrase "Jeta’s Grove and so forth," the third fascicle of the *Avadāna-sūtra* states: "In the past, there was a man who had two wives as a result of his two types of karma.

'I am young and my husband is old; I do not wish to remain here. You should go and reside at the elder wife's place.'"
Her husband pulled out the white hairs.
When he arrived at the place of his eldest wife, she said to him:
"I am old and my head has already turned white, yet your head is still black; you ought to leave."
Thereupon, he plucked out the black hairs to produce white ones.
As he did not stop doing this, his head eventually became completely bald.
His two wives detested him and each abandoned him; sitting in grief, he died.

In a past life, he was a dog in a monastery; there was one temple to the east of the river and another to the west of the river. Whenever he heard the sounding of the *gandi*, the dog would go there and obtain food.

"Because of such hesitation, he drowned in the water.
As for the mention of "Jeta-vana" in the text, it refers to the name of the monastery in general and does not specifically point to the Jeta-vana Monastery alone.
"Only the boundary, only the depth; no seeing, no attaining" summarizes the two preceding matters.

The dog heard two bells; it died solely from drowning and ultimately failed to obtain food, hence it is said that "it only drowned and did not obtain [the food].
Next, under the section "Entering the Mountains," he uses his own situation as an analogy.
One's own many obstacles are like those of a blind person or a dog.

Entering the mountains and exiting the valleys encompasses the aforementioned eight obstacles: entering the mountains subsumes the seventh and eighth, while exiting the valleys subsumes the preceding six.
"Drifting down or climbing up the river" explains the preceding phrase.

The *Wenxuan* (Selections of Refined Literature), in the "Beizheng Fu" (Rhapsody on the Northern Expedition), states: "Ascending and descending upon the ridges and hills," with the commentary noting: "'Linggang' refers to mountain mounds.

The *Huainanzi* states, "The sun enters Yanzī," with the commentary adding, "It is also called Luotáng Mountain.
The blind turtle is a metaphor for one's own lack of the eye of wisdom, while the ocean floor represents the depth of delusion.
The *Saṃyukta Āgama*, fascicle 16, states: "He addressed the bhikṣus:

Furthermore, there is a piece of floating wood with only a single hole, drifting upon the ocean waves, tossed east and west by the wind.

When a tortoise reaches the east of the sea, a floating log may reach the west of the sea; the same applies to their drifting apart or circling one another. Although they may drift apart, they might still encounter each other.
For an ordinary person to drift through the ocean of the five destinies and return again to a human body is far more difficult than this.
Now, I borrow that text as a metaphor for the difficulty of encountering a holy teacher.

The Master of the Commentary had already recited half of the scriptures by his childhood; he knew that to recite them in their entirety would require more than a single verse. Regarding the phrase "to contemplate [the karma] for the remainder of one's life":

this refers to contemplating how the karma committed in past lives has resulted in the present obstacles to the Dharma. 2. From "Matters are not [in one's own hands]" below, there are five points on the loss of his intention to retire from the world.

"The term 'que-ting' refers to the palace courtyard where the Son of Heaven resides.
